chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees, reminds them to fill out witness slips, says no food or drink is allowed, and asks everyone to turn off electronic devices. The Chair briefly notes open meetings laws before staff tells the Chair they are ready to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing with witness slip and decorum instructions

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's like open meetings laws.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you would like to testify, you must allow a witness slip with one of the sergeant arms, even if you signed up already online.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Just a reminder, there is no food or beverages allowed in this room, and please turn off all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, we are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz remarks that a staffer is his twin sister, jokes that they look identical, and thanks Amoy. He then greets everyone and begins the hearing.
chapters.title: Chair Dinowitz jokes about his twin sister before calling the hearing to order

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know we haven't started, but for the record, she's my twin sister.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We look identical twin.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But, no, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Amoy.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz identifies himself as a former public school teacher and chair of the Education Committee. He welcomes attendees to the oversight hearing on Portrait of a Graduate and asks the central question: how do you know you are doing a good job?
chapters.title: Chair Dinowitz introduces himself and frames the oversight hearing on Portrait of a Graduate

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, former public school teacher and student and proud chair of the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Welcome to today's oversight hearing on Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I firmly believe the most important element of a school system is a basic question that we talk about with our students.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says whatever gets assessed gets investment, but Regents exams do not measure what we want students to do or be. He cites ELA exams that do not require reading a whole book, global studies exams without independent research, and low algebra passing thresholds.
chapters.title: Dinowitz argues Regents exams distort what schools measure and value

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How do you know you're doing a good job?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have measures of assessment, and I see time and again that whatever gets assessed gets the investment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Whatever you're incentivized to do, you will do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But what gets measured?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The Regents exams.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yet in my time as a high school special education teacher here in our great city, it quickly became painfully clear that the Regents exam, the measure of whether or not a student graduates, never actually measured what we want our students to do

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and who we want them to be.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: ELA exams that don't actually require you to read a whole book, global studies exams that don't ask our students to conduct their own research and independently find multiple sources to support or refute a claim.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The list goes on and on.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And to make matters worse, they aren't always rigorous.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just sometimes convoluted.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Here in the city, we consider 65 passing, yet the algebra regents requires the students to earn 35% of the points to get a passing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In other words, you can get half the multiple choice questions right, none of the short answer right, and still walk away with a 62, very close to passing, but hardly a measure of whether a student deeply understands the material.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz describes the seven-year state review of graduation requirements, the Blue Ribbon Commission on graduation measures, and the July 2025 adoption of Portrait of a Graduate. He says the review found graduation measures were not serving students of color, students with disabilities, English language learners, or low-income students well.
chapters.title: Dinowitz recounts state review that led to Portrait of a Graduate

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Seven years ago, the Board of Regents and the New York State Department of Education, or NYSID,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: announced a comprehensive review of the state's high school diploma requirements.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The review concluded that the state's graduation measures were not serving all students well, and in particular were not serving students of color, students with disabilities, English language learners, and students from low-income households.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will add that the graduation requirements don't even ask what we want our students to do and be, that same questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students who engage in rigorous educational experience and use their skills to better their communities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And all the elements that we see in the schools, from journalism to music and arts,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: photography, to debate team, the debate team and math clubs, things that we know involve rigorous education, community-mindedness, civic engagement, they're not meaningfully measured by the department.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yet they are the things we are most proud of.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In our school system and when I come visit a school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's what the teachers and the principals are most proud to share.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In the years that followed NICE's decision, they gathered stakeholder input, convened a Blue Ribbon Commission on graduation measures in 2022, and received the commission's recommendations in November of 23.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz lists the six Portrait attributes: academically prepared, creative innovator, critical thinker, effective communicator, global citizen, and reflective and future-focused. He notes that students graduating in 2027-28 and later will earn a single New York State diploma without separate diploma assessment requirements.
chapters.title: Dinowitz outlines six Portrait attributes and coming diploma changes

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In July of 2025, the Board of Regents adopted the Portrait of a Graduate, or PORTRAIT, a framework describing what every public school student should know, be able to do, and embody by the time they finish high school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The aim is a system in which students can demonstrate proficiency in more than one way through options that meet the needs of all learners.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Under the portrait, a New York State graduate will expect to be, one, academically prepared, two, a creative innovator, three, a critical thinker, four, an effective communicator.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: five, global citizen, and six, reflective and future focused.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just one week ago, on September 14th, the Board of Regents authorized NYSA to move forward with the remaining pieces of this transition beginning in the 27-28 school year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students graduating in 27-28 school year or later will earn a single New York State diploma without separate diploma assessment requirements.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says Regents exams are not disappearing completely and will remain as measures of state learning standards and federal accountability. What is ending is the requirement that students pass them to earn a diploma, with districts expected to use locally developed assessment strategies.
chapters.title: Dinowitz clarifies Regents exams will remain but no longer be required for graduation

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That means today's high school seniors are the last class who will have to pass the Regents exam in order to graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I see no one upset by this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Regents exams are not disappearing completely.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: NICET has said the exams will remain as measures of achievement of state learning standards, and state assessments will continue to be administered to satisfy federal requirements under Every Student Succeeds Act.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is ending is the requirement that students pass them to earn a diploma.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In its place, districts will be expected to assess students according to local developed strategies.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the shift puts a great deal of weight on the NYC Department of Education and notes the state timeline is incomplete. He lists questions for the hearing: what is being done now for students in grades 9-11, expanding work-based learning, learning from consortium schools, and coordinating with NYSED.
chapters.title: Dinowitz highlights DOE implementation gaps and questions for hearing

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This shift puts a great deal of weight on the New York City Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: NYSID's own transformation timeline schedules the release of portrait rubrics and guidance for this school year, and NYSID has committed to releasing additional implementation guidance by summer 2027.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Regulatory amendments to Part 100 of the Commissioner's regulations are not scheduled to reach the Board as a discussion item until February of 27, with adoption anticipated in June of 27.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As of last week, advocates were telling the regents that schools still do not know how they will measure proficiency for students currently in grades 9 through 11, students who will be affected in less than a year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Implementing this vision across the nation's largest school district will be an enormous undertaking.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And New York City will be doing it on a timeline the state has not fully yet defined.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In March, Chancellor Samuel signaled that the DOE plans to ramp up its work on portrait and restructured his cabinet to create a senior position supervising high school leadership.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That division was filled.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: By Dr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Alan Cheng, who previously oversaw Outward Bound Schools, the Internationals Network, serving newcomer immigrant students, and New York Performance Standards Consortium Schools, a portfolio that includes some of New York City's most established performance assessment models.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Beyond that appointment, the DOE has not publicly announced an implementation plan

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: professional development program, or guidance to schools on the portrait.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So today we will ask, how is the city preparing to implement the portrait framework across New York City public schools?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is being done now for students in grades 9 through 11 and beyond?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And who will graduate under the new system?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are you expanding work-based learning and other performance-based opportunities in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What are you learning from consortium schools which have assessed students this way for decades?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how are you coordinating with NYSID on these issues?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the Portrait could radically transform schools or become a compliance checklist that sacrifices quality education for graduation rates. He thanks committee members and staff for their work on the hearing.
chapters.title: Dinowitz warns Portrait could become compliance checklist or lose rigor

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The portrait has the ability to radically transform our school system in a way that will finally allow our schools to fully invest in programs that we know actually benefit students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And allow our students to display their vast knowledge and skills in ways unconstrained by poorly written or poorly graded Regents exams.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do, however, fear the portrait runs the risk of removing all rigor from our school system by doing what we so often do in the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Turn a well-meaning policy into a compliance checklist, and allow the DOE pressures to improve graduation rates and credit accrual at the expense of quality education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The future of our school system and therefore our city

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: rests on our ability to properly implement this directive.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I look forward to today's important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I also want to thank the members of the Education Committee who have joined us today, including Council Members De La Rosa, Gutierrez, Lewis, Narcisse, Lee, Wong, and Joseph.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz thanks staff, reminds witnesses to fill out slips, says there will be no voting today, and limits testimony to two minutes and council questions to five minutes. He administers the affirmation to mayoral administration witnesses and tells them they may begin.
chapters.title: Chair outlines hearing logistics, witness limits, and administers affirmation

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And on Zoom, we have Count Amaris Farias and Zhuang.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would also like to thank my Chief of Staff, Jenna Klaus, my Legislative and Budget Director, Theo Solter, and the Education Committee staff.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: including Senior Legislative Counsel Alejandro Carvajal, Senior Legislative Policy Analyst Chloe Rivera, Legislative Policy Analyst Katie Salina,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Principal Financial Analyst Andrew Lane Lawless and Financial Analyst Grace Amato for their work on today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would like to remind everyone who wishes to testify in person today that you must fill out a witness slip, which you can find on the desk of the Sergeant at Arms near the entrance of this room.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please fill out the slip even if you have already registered in advance that you will be testifying in person today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I also want to point out that we will not be voting on legislation today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: To allow as many people as possible to testify, testimony will be limited to two minutes per person, whether you are testifying in person or on Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I am also going to ask my colleagues to limit their questions and comments to five minutes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please note that generally, witnesses who are here in person will testify before those who are here on the Zoom webinar.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As a reminder to all of our witnesses, please state your name prior to your testimony for the record.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If anyone here requires an accessible version of a presentation given at today's hearing, please email testimony at council.nyc.gov.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, in accordance with the rules of the council, I will administer the affirmation to the witnesses from the mayoral administration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will call on each of you individually for your response.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The record show they all said yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, and you may begin your testimony.

chapters.summary: Giunta introduces herself and her colleagues from NYC Public Schools, including Dr. Alan Cheng, Jane Martinez-Dowling, Cordelia Veve, Katie Hansen, Sharon Rensher, and Michael Prayor. She thanks the Council and begins describing the statewide effort that started with the 2019 Blue Ribbon Commission on Graduation Measures.
chapters.title: First Deputy Chancellor Danielle Giunta introduces DOE panel and frames NY Inspires

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dinowitz, members of the committee, and distinguished members of City Council.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: My name is Danielle Junta, and I'm the first deputy chancellor of New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleagues, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Alan Chang, supervising superintendent of high schools in District 79.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Jane Martinez-Dowling, Chief of Student Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Cordelia Veve, Chief of Curriculum and Instruction.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Katie Hansen, Executive Director of Academic Policy and Systems.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Sharon Rensher, Senior Executive Director of State and Federal Education Policy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And planning, and Michael Preyer, our superintendent of Brooklyn South High Schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to talk about the implementation of New York Inspires and New York State's Portrait of a Graduate framework.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This statewide effort started back in 2019 with the New York State Blue Ribbon Commission on Graduation Measures, which brought together educators, students,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: families, higher education leaders, employers, community representatives, to examine whether New York State's graduation system was preparing students for success in a rapidly changing world.

chapters.summary: Giunta says more than 20 states are reexamining graduation requirements to align with college, careers, and civic life. She describes New York Inspires as an invitation to rethink what it means for a student to graduate prepared, and asks what every student should know, be able to do, and be prepared for.
chapters.title: Giunta places NY Inspires in national movement and explains its purpose

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The resulting recommendations laid the foundation for New York Inspires and Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: New York's work is part of a growing national movement, with more than 20 states across the country reexamining graduation requirements to better align with the knowledge, skills, and experiences students need for college, careers, and civic life.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: While approaches vary by state, a common theme has emerged, maintaining rigorous academic expectations while creating more opportunities for students to demonstrate learning through authentic, real-world

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: experiences and multiple measures of readiness.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: New York Inspires, New York's statewide effort, invites us to rethink what it means for a student to graduate from high school prepared for college, career, and civic life.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We at New York City Public Schools are embracing this opportunity to actualize the mayor and chancellor's vision for how New York City Public Schools can best serve New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In our schools, we believe this work is ultimately about a simple but important question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What should every student know, be able to do, and be prepared for when they leave schools?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The world our students are entering is changing rapidly.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Advances in technology, new economic demands, and evolving career pathways require students to possess

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: not only strong academic knowledge, but also the ability to think critically, communicate effectively, solve complex problems, work collaboratively, and adapt to change.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: These are not new aspirations.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They are skills that families, employers, colleges, and educators have long valued.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What is new is our opportunity to ensure they are consistently developed and recognized across a student's entire educational journey.

chapters.summary: Giunta says the Portrait of a Graduate was adopted in 2025 and shifts the conversation from what students complete to what they can demonstrate. She says this is not about lowering expectations but raising them, with examples like oral defenses, capstones, and portfolios, while academic rigor in core subjects remains essential.
chapters.title: Giunta says Portrait raises expectations and expands ways to demonstrate learning

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The New York State Portrait of a Graduate was adopted by New York City Public Schools in 2025 and provides a shared vision for that future.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It shifts the conversation beyond what students complete and toward what students can demonstrate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It asks us to create learning experiences that help young people become academically prepared, creative innovators, critical thinkers, effective communicators, global citizens, and reflective and future-focused learners.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Importantly, this work is not about lowering expectations.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It is about raising them.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: For too long, a single measure has carried outsized weight in determining how readiness is defined.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Under New York Inspire, students will increasingly be asked to demonstrate their learning in authentic and meaningful ways.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They will be expected to apply knowledge, explain their thinking, solve authentic problems, and show evidence of growth and achievement over time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This could look like an eighth grader being asked to do an oral defense rather than

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: just taking a test to demonstrate their academic knowledge as well as effective communication and critical thinking, two of our portrait of a graduate attributes.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our goal is to expand opportunities that for one, that one for real world demonstrations of learning, capstones and portfolios, for instance.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Across New York City public schools, many schools already provide students with opportunities to demonstrate their learning in these effective ways, and we strive to expand that access.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Academic rigor remains essential.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: As we expand academic foundations to include personal finance and climate education, we are not moving away from robust and rigorous literacy, math, science, social studies, and the arts.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They represent critical disciplinary knowledge and skills that students need to be successful.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Furthermore, our work through New York City Reads and New York City Solves provides the essential instructional foundation on which we are building our implementation of the portrait of a graduate and New York's inspires.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Shared research-based curricula that ensure every student engages in grade-level learning,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: coupled with sustained professional learning and support for educators, will remain central to improving student achievement and preparing students to apply their knowledge and skills in meaningful ways.

chapters.summary: Giunta says moving beyond test scores as the sole measurement raises expectations. She says decoupling Regents from graduation opens doors for multiple demonstrations of learning, and NYCPS will build on student pathways, work-based learning, and affinity partnerships. She notes full implementation is targeted for 2029-30.
chapters.title: Giunta says decoupling Regents is a major opportunity and outlines multi-year rollout

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Moving beyond test scores as the sole measurement for student learning is an opportunity to raise expectations for our students.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Even though the regents are not going away,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Decoupling them from graduation requirements starting next year is a profound opportunity and major change.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It opens the door more widely for students to authentically and in multiple ways demonstrate their learning and readiness to graduate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are excited about the opportunity New York Inspires brings for our students in New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we look forward to continuing our partnership with New York State Education Department on the rollout, as well as sharing what we see for the future with our students, educators, and families.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are approaching this work with humility and optimism because we are not starting from scratch.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: New York Inspires is a multi-year design and implementation effort.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: When it is at full implementation in 2930, we will have spent years laying the foundation for our students'success.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We will build on the success of Office of Student Pathways innovations such as our STEAM centers, early colleges, P-TECH, and career and technical education schools, and the transformative, evidence-based, future-ready New York City.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Which is in over a third of our high schools and has a proven efficacy with substantial impact data.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We will continue to scale and sustain student pathways to increase participation in career-connected learning, such as work-based learning programs and apprenticeships, while deepening our investments in industry-aligned pathways with the support of both public sector and

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: industry champions in healthcare,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: education, building trades, and sustainable green economy.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: These examples

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: show us that rigorous, engaging, future-focused learning is already taking place throughout our system.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our responsibility now is to learn from those successes, build on them, and create conditions that allow more students to benefit from similar opportunities.

chapters.summary: Giunta says every student in every neighborhood should have access to high-quality learning experiences and that equity must remain central. She says NYCPS will engage educators, families, students, higher education partners, employers, community organizations, and elected officials, and closes by thanking the Council.
chapters.title: Giunta commits to equity, communication, and engaging stakeholders

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are approaching this work with a clear commitment.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Every student in every neighborhood should have access to high-quality learning experiences that prepare them for the opportunities and challenge of the future.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Equity must remain at the center of this transformation.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The promise of New York Inspires is not that a few schools will innovate while others remain unchanged.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The promise is that all students will benefit from stronger connections between classroom learning and the knowledge, skills, and experiences they need to thrive beyond graduation.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: As we move forward, New York City Public Schools is committed to engaging educators, families, students, higher education partners, employers, community organizations, and elected officials in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Lasting educational transformation succeeds only when it is grounded in trust, transparency, and shared understanding.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Families deserve clear information about what these changes mean for their children.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Educators deserve the support necessary to implement new approaches while maintaining high expectations.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And students deserve a system that recognizes their strengths and prepares them for their next steps.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our goal is simply not to respond to policy changes at the state level.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want to take this opportunity for the largest school district.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: district in the country to show what's possible when we innovate and bring authentic, real-world learning into our classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Our goal is to ensure that a diploma from New York City Public Schools continues to be a meaningful symbol of achievement and readiness.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want graduates to leave our schools with strong academic foundations, confidence in their abilities, opportunities to pursue their aspirations, and the skills necessary to contribute to their communities and our city.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: New York Inspires presents a historic opportunity to align our educational system around a shared vision for student success from the earliest grades through graduation.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: While this work will take time, we are excited about its potential to better prepare young people for the future they will inherit and help shape.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We look forward to answering any questions and continue our partnership to ensure that New York City student graduates are ready to learn, lead, contribute, and succeed.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says principals, teachers, and parents lack guidance about what Portrait looks like in practice. He asks what work the DOE has done to date to plan for implementation. Giunta describes engagement with the Blue Ribbon Commission and trainings for superintendents and principals.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE what work has been done to plan Portrait implementation

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilmember Krishnan.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So, First Deputy Chancellor, keep getting that seat, the Chancellor, First Deputy Chancellor.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think you spoke in broad strokes about some of the ideas about Portrait of a Graduate, and so I want to dig into, I guess, what it looks like in practice.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to share some general concerns.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'll ask a question, but just to share the concerns I'm hearing from principals, they haven't gotten much guidance about what it actually looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Though principals say, well, I have these great programs and I think it fits into these categories.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Teachers who need to be trained on how to shift their curriculum or include or exclude things that they would have otherwise done don't know where they're going because they don't know how they'll be assessed, how the students will be assessed, what guidance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And parents often have no idea what we're talking about when we say the portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So when I hear you say families deserve clear information about what these changes mean, educators deserve, I agree with you, and that's why I think the hearing is important today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Let's really dig down on this information.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So what work has the DOE done to date to plan for implementing the portrait of the graduate framework?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have, we've been engaging in a lot of work around Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It started with Sharon Renter's membership and partnership with the state and the Blue Ribbon Commission on which so many of our folks participated.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And then as it came into New York City schools, we worked with Katie's team in the Office of Policy and Evaluation to

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: put together trainings for our superintendents, their deputies, their senior cabinets, and every principal across the system.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz interrupts to ask what schools are currently doing Portrait work. Giunta backs up to explain system-readiness efforts, then turns to Dr. Alan Cheng to describe the core team and steering committee leading the work.
chapters.title: Dinowitz presses on which schools are currently doing Portrait work

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can I pause one second just to...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What you said came into the schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What schools are currently doing portrait of a graduate work?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: All right, let me back out.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So let me answer some of the question around what have we been doing to get the system ready for portrait of graduate?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is really what I'm seeking to answer first.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And then to your question, we have...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Similar to the district that Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Chang was leading, lots of robust examples and the work of Students Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This work is in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But first, let us back out into what the plan is and how we've been approaching it in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So I'll start with Alan Chang talking a little bit about our core team, our steering committee, and then Katie can talk a little bit about the content that we've been making sure our

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: superintendents, their teams, and all of our principals have engaged in.

chapters.summary: Cheng says NYC already has a head start through Future Ready NYC and affinity partners. He says DOE has brought together superintendents and principals for 45 meetings on the timeline and six essential proficiencies, and is doing asset mapping and planning citywide professional learning.
chapters.title: Alan Cheng describes DOE steering committee and professional learning for Portrait

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I'm Alan Chang, Supervising Superintendent for High Schools in District 79.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Really want to start by thanking you for convening this committee and giving us a chance to be able to answer some of these questions because this is such an important part of the direction that we're going in.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I also want to be able to acknowledge that, as you stated, that there's such tremendous work that is already happening in our system.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We have networks of schools that have been deeply committed to career and technical education through Future Ready NYC.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We have many members of our affinity partners and schools that have been doing this work.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And there are so many elements that we are already seeing that are giving us a head start as part of this.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: New York State has also recognized that this is a multi-year transition.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: They do not expect this to be a switch that gets flipped in overnight.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We will later talk about sort of each of the years and cohorts and exactly what that means.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We're also, of course, committed to working directly with our superintendents, our principals, and our teachers through our existing professional development structures to be able to help them deeply grapple with.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You have journalism students who believe in a free press.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please don't cut his mic.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Let's use this one.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: No, you should be fine.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: There we go.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We're back on.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: All right, perfect.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We're back on.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: You know, for a while there, you get to your teacher voice, your principal voice, and you can do that.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So I do want to be able to say that we have many professional learning structures that are going to be really important.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So far in the last six months, one of the key things that we can speak to is that we have brought together

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: every one of our superintendents to be able to go deeply into and understanding what this timeline looks like, what are the six essential proficiencies that are part of a portrait of a graduate, as well as the implications for each of the coming cohorts.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Once we've done that, we then went into our superintendent meetings with their principals.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We held 45 meetings, each with each group and district, so community school districts as well as high school districts, presenting to them, here's the basic information that the state has laid out.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Let's do some asset mapping around what are the key qualities that your schools already have in place?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: What is the capacity of your district team to be able to support our schools?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And then what are some practices that you want to be able to grow in and how do we design that?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We took that feedback.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: gather that information.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And we're also working very closely with the state to be able to design specific

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: citywide professional learnings that we will be opening up to our schools and our teachers so that they can really help inform what this process will look like moving forward.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says principals and teachers have heard broad strokes and timelines but not what Portrait looks like in the classroom. He asks what rigorous experiential learning actually looks like and how it differs from a regular class project.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks for classroom-level examples, not just timelines

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I want to kind of summarize a little bit so far for that question of what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Asset mapping, you've gone to all your high schools, or are you focused on sort of your PBATs, like your old schools?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So what we have done is we've met with every single superintendent, and the superintendents run their principal meetings.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so this spring, we met with every single principal, not just the high schools, not just the high schools in my former district, but really across the system.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I want to turn it over to Katie Hansen, who can also speak a little bit more about some additional continued engagement that we've been doing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to try to be focused.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to get away from the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm communicating to you what teachers, principals, administrators, superintendents have communicated to me, that they've gotten a lot on the timeline, a lot on the broad strokes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But not really a lot on what it looks like in the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like what is a rigorous experiential learning and how does that differ from just like a regular class project that a teacher might do, you know, a two-day little project.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So if you can incorporate that, I would appreciate that as well.

chapters.summary: Dowling says personal finance launched this year for grades 5-12, with 50% of middle and high school students scheduled for fall instruction. She describes vetted curriculum options, district point people, and summer institute training for 1,600 educators.
chapters.title: Jane Martinez-Dowling details personal finance rollout as first phase-two requirement

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think I'll transition.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, this year we know that personal finance actually launched in our schools as a part of this.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that world lives within our Office of Student Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And Jane can talk a little bit about how that is getting off the ground so that we can talk more about how this is actually hitting schools, the supports that they've received, and what's going on in that first phase in of personal finance.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Thank you, FTC.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And it's good to see many of you.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So as part of the phase two rollout of New York Inspires, we've adopted the Board of Regents adopted a K-12 personal finance education requirement.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And that's the first one that is going to be effective this year.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: fall, the fall of 2026-27, for grades 5 through 12, and then in the following year for grades K through 4.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Because financial literacy has traditionally sat within our career-connected learning through Future Ready,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: we took on the task this summer through our summer institute where we see 1,600 educators and we talk to them about what the portrait of a graduate will look like in their schools,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: really kind of set everyone up to do their personal finance education.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It's really important because personal finance helps our students prepare financially.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We are coupling it with a lot of the work that we're doing with Save for College, which also lives in our portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And we want to really support the long-term economic mobility as students navigate increasingly complex financial decisions.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you how to run a Robin Hood app, but our kids are going to have to know that.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And so we took a proactive system-wide approach ahead of implementation.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Each superintendent designated a district point person.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Schools received vetted curriculum options and implementation guidance, and personal finance was a major focus, as I said, of our summer institute.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Implementation is still in its early stages, but nearly 50% of our middle and high school students have personal finance instruction scheduled for the fall semester,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: with additional schools expected to provide instruction during the spring semester based on their scheduling.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: what their scheduling model looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can I pause there?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Middle and high school students, how many have it programmed for their,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: 50% of middle and high school students have it in their personal finance instruction that's scheduled for the fall.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like this year?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: This year, starting in September.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there a state or city curriculum that is official and being used?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: What we did was that we provided schools with a menu of centrally reviewed curriculum resources

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: aligned to the New York State five required personal finance learning targets, while allowing students the flexibility to select the option that best fits their local context.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there, and this is going to conform with like this portfolio-based or project-based learning, like that idea?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Yes, it will fit in within one of the many attributes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And are there sample assignments or specific assignments per the curriculum that students have to complete?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or are you relying on the teachers to come up with those?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: No, we actually have those because the implementation models that we have used are those that we have been using through the Office of Student Pathways when we've been implementing financial literacy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So the projects or portfolio, the assignment themselves exist.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I assume then that the rubric exists and it's across all of the schools.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Why don't...

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Do you want me...

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: I'm happy to tell you what the implementation structure looks like in all of those schools.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: From grades 5 through 8 and grades 9 through 12, schools may provide instruction through a designated course, embedded instruction, a CTE pathway, or a combination of approaches.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: As a result, implementation may occur during different grades or semester, depending on the school's academic program and scheduling structures.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And as students progress through their different grade bands, you know, to make it developmentally appropriate, instruction becomes increasingly sophisticated, helping them build and apply knowledge related to earning, spending, saving, credit, risk, and other financial decisions.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We at New York City Public Schools are going to continue supporting schools through professional learning, technical assistance, and borough-based communities of practice throughout the school year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think one of the concerns people have about taking away the regents is like them or hate them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like a teacher knows kind of like what they have to teach and everyone's graded essentially the same way.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think people are looking for the same thing with whatever assignments.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to make sure that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This program, the financial literacy, and we'll have other programs, but focus on financial literacy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The assessments are the same across the board, or they're the same per curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is the rubric the same across the board per grade level?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like, will every ninth grader be assessed using the same rubric?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Rubric.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That way, as an employer, I know that a kid who took, you know, the financial literacy at one school has passed the same meaningful assessment as at any other school in the city.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if a 10th grader in Brooklyn using EverFi will be assessed on the same standards as a student in the Bronx. Dowling says standards are the same but implementation models and assessments vary, and Cheng adds that DOE is norming and scoring across schools to ensure consistency.
chapters.title: Dinowitz questions whether personal finance assessments and rubrics are consistent citywide

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Well, it's going to depend on the model used, right?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So we have five different models that students can select from.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So within that curriculum, let's say curriculum A, call it whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: EverFi is one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is it called?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: EverFi.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: EverFi?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Cool.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: EverFi.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: EverFi.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: That's just one of the five.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, EverFi.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's a silly name.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: I didn't make the brand.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It's just, you know what I mean?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Ah, but you bought it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just kidding.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What I'm saying is like a kid who goes to EverFi 10th grade in Brooklyn is going to have the same assessment or be assessed on the same standards as a kid in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's a yes.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: The standards will be the same, but as Dr.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Chang said, it's going to depend on the model used, and it's going to depend on what schools are using.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So a student can be assessed through quizzes, through projects, through performance tasks, through case studies, presentations, or other classroom-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: But what we are doing is we are using...

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Models that actually hit all of the standards that the state has told us are important for personal finance.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how is the DOE ensuring that the rigor remains?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think this question is similar to any other subject.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How is the DOE ensuring what work has been done to ensure that the rigor remains, that students are graded, whatever the method of assessment is, on some sort of standard so we know it's transferable from school to school.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: I mean, I'm happy to say that these are all models that we have used through our own work at the Office of Student Pathways, but I'm happy to turn it over to one of our colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It's still being developed, right?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: This will be the first year, but what we do...

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: know is that all of the five that we selected were one because of schools and high schools and superintendents and principals that were very interested and had proven efficacy on the models

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: and second that there was an opportunity to really figure out like how is what is the best way to ensure that my students in my schools are learning the competencies.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Chang?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think at the core of your question is when we have these standards and expectations, how are we able to hold that level of expectations and that rigor across our schools?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And I think that that's a completely fair question for us to be asking at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so I want to be able to highlight that across all of these curriculums, we've made abundantly clear what the state standards are.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: In the curriculum are tasks, assessment practices, and rubrics in which we are providing ongoing training.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: In addition to that, we bring together teachers, ensure that what it is that they are grading and assessing are normed and scored.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so you're familiar with how we do region-based scoring on open-ended assessments.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: There are similar practices that says whether or not this particular task should result in this particular kind of score.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: That kind of norm referencing is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And to be able to ensure that we're being transparent.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: about the standards that we're asking our students to do.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So in the case of personal finance, we are following what the state has laid out in terms of what the standards,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: we've ensured that the curriculum layer is fully aligned, and we are doing the norming that is necessary across our schools to make sure that what this particular teacher says, this is great work, you've learned the standards, is also true in the next school.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz shares concern that without a rigorous replacement for Regents, schools may receive pressure to pass students through credit accrual alone. He says standardized rubrics and norming are critical to maintaining quality across the city.
chapters.title: Dinowitz warns against pressure to pass students without rigor

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just, I have to say it because I remember during COVID when we got pressure to pass kids who never showed up to class.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I remember hearing administrators before COVID.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I remember one administrator said to a teacher, well, I know they didn't do the final project, but can you pass them?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And they promised to do the assignment over the summer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: One of those is anecdotal, but one of those was like a systemic sort of directive.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And to hear that is good, that the training is happening is good and heartening to hear because that's what rigor looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And maintaining that and making sure that it is normed and that there are standardized rubrics across the city, I think is really critical to making sure not just personal finance, but if that model is used for

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: other subjects, that's a good start.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, I have a ton more questions, but I do want to turn it over to colleagues for their questions.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks if DOE has a written implementation plan and when it will be released publicly. Giunta describes a cross-office core team and steering committee, and Katie Hansen says the steering committee has about 20 members including superintendents and representatives from central offices.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph asks about written implementation plan and steering committee

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we'll start with Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I know I have five minutes, so I'm going to ask a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Beyond creating the senior supervising superintendent position, does DOE have a written implementation plan, and when will it be released publicly?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes, we have our supervising superintendent here.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Some structures that we have stood up centrally is a core team, which is widely represented here by the various offices under the division of the first deputy chancellor that are influencing and delivering this work from Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Chang to Office of Student Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It is a very heavily seated academic policy, so we have OPE with us today.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Of course, academics and instruction as well.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This is a beautiful cross-office partnership.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This group has also been leading a steering committee that widens the voice and feedback that we're getting.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: How many people are on the steering committee?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: How many are on the steering committee?

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: It's about 20.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: We have representatives from the teams that First Deputy Chancellor named, Division of Inclusive and Accessible Learning, our communications team, as well as several of our superintendents.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And we use that to norm on the updates we're getting from the state, make sure we have a shared understanding of the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And we also use it as a group for thought partnership and developing a strategy around each of these components of the New York Constitution.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks what safeguards exist for multilingual learners and students with disabilities, noting they often account for graduation declines. Giunta says multiple measures will help these students demonstrate knowledge in new ways and that the DIALL team is included in planning professional learning.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how DOE safeguards Portrait assessments for multilingual learners and students with disabilities

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And students, multilingual learners and students with disabilities usually statewide account for the decline in graduation.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What safeguards do you have in place to make sure that local portrait assessments are created for these students?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I mean, at its core, this opportunity to move away from a single measurement for graduation into multiple measurements is a place that is going to really help our students with disabilities and multilingual learners show

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and demonstrate their knowledge in new and exciting ways that will honor their knowledge and the way that they can express it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: To Katie's point, have our dial colleagues on the team with us.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And as we plan professional learning with them, just like with reads and solves, the dial team is with us, making sure that the lens of the students that they support are very well represented in how we move forward.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And I did want to mention that in addition to the structures that we set up, the professional learning that Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Chang talked about and some of the early implementation as it relates to personal finance,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: there is a lot of information widely available on the state's website about this that parents can access, but we are currently getting ready to pull it over to our website in addition to the work and the values that New York City Public Schools has

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and move into a more New York City engagement around this topic.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Last week's meeting with the state and this week's...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: hearing is certainly helping catapult that aligned timeline to make this really a robust conversation across our city.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks for the specific professional development plan, budget, and number of schools that have received Portrait-aligned training. Giunta says the summer institute reached 1,600 educators and that DOE is leveraging existing resources rather than creating a standalone Portrait budget.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about professional development plan, budget, and number of schools trained

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What specific professional development plan and budget and how many schools have received portrait aligned training so far?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What are your numbers?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I wouldn't say outside of the personal finance work, all of the work that lives under, actually, let me, there's a lot because of the work that Jane leads.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And to the point she shared before, reaching over 1,600 educators over the summer institute, which was very strongly aligned to Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, I just want to reiterate that we believe that at the foundation of Portrait of a Graduate is our New York City Reads and Solves approach to having high quality instructional materials in our classrooms.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Making sure we have strong assessments that catch students that might be in need of additional supports and having very clear interventions that align with their needs.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so with that also comes a tremendous amount of professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And then we also have, I shared on the steps earlier, you know, as a superintendent who led one of the city's first civics for all district partnerships, I think we are at almost

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: 30 something partner districts at this point.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so much of that work comes with professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So what we're doing now is not necessarily like this dedicated portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: budget and standalone professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We're taking all the things that we do as it aligns into this framework and helping our schools, leveraging existing resources and initiatives.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we're not layering more.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We're having people step back and say, here's where the action is.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So I'm running out of time.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Do you want another question?

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how DOE will communicate with students and parents in the first affected cohorts. Giunta says DOE is entering its communications plan now and will share the timeline and expectations, while noting current graduation measures remain until the state formalizes changes.
chapters.title: Joseph asks about public communication plan for class of 2027 and 2028

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I have another question, of course.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What is the DOE's public communication plan for students and parents, particularly the class of 2027 and 2028, the first cohort that will be affected.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Well, we are entering into our communications plan now so that we can very clearly lay out exactly, I guess that goes back to Chair Dinowitz's, the timeline.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We want to make sure our families know the timeline and the expectations.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But the state is clear until more formal information and structures and directions come out, we are operating under the current graduation measures.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how NYC can build on Future Ready, career readiness, and apprenticeship programs. Dowling describes existing infrastructure including work-based learning, CTE, Learning to Work, industry commissions, and partnerships with DYCD and DCAS.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how DOE will build on career-connected learning investments

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And as New York City implement the portrait of a graduate, how can the city build on sustained investments in existing models like Future Ready, Career Readiness, Modern Youth Apprentice, and what students that give students opportunities to develop, demonstrate these

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: through career connected learning, paid experience and apprenticeship?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I mean, I'm going to turn that over to Jane.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: This is her topic and passion.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Higher Education Chair Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: You have to do the flip back and forth.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Happens all the time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Tids and Wits is not offended.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So as you know, we've already built a lot of the infrastructure needed to scale our work through a work-based learning through Future Ready, CTE, Learning to Work, which is helpful to the population that you were speaking to,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: our industry commissions, intermediary partners, and as you all know, we have a really strong collaboration with DYCD, DCAS, and then the Office of Talent and Workforce Development.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: If work-based learning becomes a primary demonstration of proficiency, there are going to be three things that are critical.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: One is that we have clear standards and assessment rubrics, so schools, employers, and students have a shared definition of what proficiency looks like and how it's going to be measured.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Second is that we have to build capacity for schools through training, tools, and implementation support to ensure consistent high-quality assessment of student learning.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And really important to that, schools also have to have employer support.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Teachers, workplace learning coordinators, and workplace supervisors need clear tools, examples, training.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And proof points, right, to make sure that students are receiving a strong experience.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: and are evaluated fairly.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And then the third thing, again, which you spoke to, is just making sure that there's equity, innovation, and sustained investment to ensure that all the students have access to high-quality work-based learning opportunities,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: including students in every borough, students with learning differences, multilingual learners,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: and immigrant students.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: This includes funding for paid work-based learning experiences because we really believe that our students really deserve to be paid for the time that they're investing and for innovative models to help schools and employers expand

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: access while maintaining quality at scale.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We do have a really strong foundation to build from with Career Ready, SYEP, Work and Learn and Grow, Future Ready NYC, and CTE, which already connect thousands of students to career-connected experience.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We have about 90,000 students who are already receiving work-based learning experiences to provide a platform for future scale.

chapters.summary: Joseph asks how DOE measures success of work-based learning. Dowling cites outcomes including increased college enrollment, $85 million in wages and tuition savings over five years, and employer feedback on the value students add in workplaces.
chapters.title: Joseph asks how DOE will measure success of work-based learning as proficiency demonstration

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And like Chair Denwiss would say, how do we measure success?

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: What's the plan to measure success in all of that that you've said?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So because we have been working with our work-based learning students and their experiences, we have seen some very strong outcomes around the impact of work-based learning.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It is impacting students going to secondary schools.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It's increased the number of college, students are teaching college now courses.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And really importantly, our kids have earned $85 million over the past five years, both in tuition savings and also in direct wages.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We believe that those are actually pretty strong impacts.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And then the work and the growth that employers are telling us, both in the public sector and the private sector, about how these students, through either apprenticeships or the internships that they're doing, have really, really added value to the work that's happening in their

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: places of work.
