chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if DOE intends different standards for students with disabilities under Portrait, as was the case with some Regents flexibilities. Alan Cheng says all students will be held to high standards, rubrics set expectations, and multiple ways to demonstrate learning with accommodations, but not lower standards.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks whether students with disabilities will have different standards or rubrics

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to ask, I just have one question because it was brought up about students with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: With the Regents exams, students with disabilities, students with an IEP, did not necessarily have to pass every Regents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They could do a combination of getting a little lower than a 65, right, if they made up for it in other tests.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The details of which I don't remember, that's the general sense, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There was sort of different standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is the intention of the DOE to similarly have different standards for students with disabilities?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or will students with disabilities be held to the same rigorous standards as students without an IEP?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: All of our students need to be held to extremely high standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That was a good answer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: My question, that was a great answer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: My question is, will there be a different rubric for students with disabilities, or will they be held to the same rubric?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You can use that language.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think what the rubrics do is they set the expectation.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think what's really important that our schools do and their teachers do is to really lean into this idea that there are multiple forms of assessment and multiple ways for the students to be able to demonstrate what it is that they know.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So you have the standards.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: You have the rubric that lays out in the plain language.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And then we say to students, what are the different ways that we think is crucial for you to be able to demonstrate that?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And we have a long history of doing that here in the city.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And in fact, when we move away, when we begin to decouple the exams, we begin to say there are many other ways for the students to be able to demonstrate that particular skill.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just want to pause.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's one of the reasons I love the idea of the portrait.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But we have seen on IEPs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A student has to get 30.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: percent of the third, fourth, fifth grade curriculum, often to, I believe, to their detriment, because then they get to the later grades in the high school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We don't have that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We can't say, or we shouldn't say, they need to only get a 30% on the regions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What we do have is saying, essentially, you don't have to get the same scores as your classmates without an IEP.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm simply asking if it's the intention of the DOE to say student disabilities, every other kid has to get, you know, at least eight out of 10 on this project, you only have to get a seven or a combination.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or is the intention to say the standards are the standards because it's project-based learning, there's more time to work on this and the standards are the same with or without an IEP.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What's the intention?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: The intention is the latter part of what he said, which is these are the standards.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: There are multiple ways of being able to meet that.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: For example, if we're thinking about career and technical education, if we're going to train somebody to be an electrician, to be a medical assisting, we want to make sure they are meeting the same bar.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And it's incumbent upon us to work with our students, their learning styles, their IEP needs, ensure the proper accommodations are in place.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: But the standards absolutely have to be as high as ever.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether curriculum design support at the school level is mandatory or volunteer. Giunta says DOE is not bringing in new curriculum but using existing NYC Reads and Solves materials and professional learning to rethink delivery and assessment.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse asks how DOE supports school-level curriculum design

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Madam Deputy, and all your leadership here with you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: One of the things that got me excited as a parent, I had to go through four kids, I think from...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Doctorate from this and that and the third.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm so appreciative in the time of AI that our children is not really can solve their own problem, their own disagreement.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Effective communicators.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know we don't have that with the journalism here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Where are the young folks?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They're gone probably.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Anyways, I'm so happy that we're incorporating all that right now to make sure our kids are successful.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Coming to the teaching, to the teachers'training and professional development, I want to know, so how is DOE supporting the curriculum we design at the school level?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that support mandatory or volunteer?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So right now there's no reason to necessarily do like a curriculum redesign.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are not bringing in new curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What is exciting for our teachers as they move into the, like the, what are we in year four of New York City Reads for some of our schools, year three or in solves.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And our social studies and science, all of it is to think about, here's our core curriculum, here's our high quality instruction materials, and with our professional learning partners,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: thinking more about the pedagogy, the delivery of this content, what opportunities in our curriculum

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and in the standards our students need, can we deliver this maybe differently so that students have more opportunities to effectively communicate or demonstrate their learning than just even an end-of-unit exam?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Those are next steps.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: For us to tackle.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have so many professional learning partners in our schools that are both external through Reads and Solves, but internal by way of district teams, by our lead teachers and our

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: masterful principals that we can tap into the knowledge base that exists across New York City to help them rethink how they're delivering.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, in Reads,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: alone, the modules are, regardless of the three different curricular choices, they are centered around these essential questions.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we want to help our teachers think about how we can bring these units to life more dynamically.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is what New York Inspires and Portrait of a Graduate is giving us permission to do, and that will be

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: some of the ways we think about the supports our teachers need in the delivery and how students are experiencing the curriculum as an exit.

chapters.summary: Narcisse reports that families and students do not know what is required of them anymore. Giunta asks Katie Hansen to break down the timeline clearly for families.
chapters.title: Narcisse says parents and students are confused about graduation requirements

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now I'm already hearing from my office, from parents and students who doesn't know what's required of them anymore.

utterances.text: You know, we are seeing too that

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Really very clearly say exactly how this

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: but for now katie can you just crystal clear for us uh what to expect over the next few years sure thank you

chapters.summary: Hansen says current seniors still graduate against 44 credits and generally five exams. If the Board of Regents adopts changes, current juniors and below will graduate without Regents exams, and the advanced Regents diploma remains an option. The new transcript is targeted for 2029-30.
chapters.title: Katie Hansen clarifies graduation timeline: no impact this year, decoupling next year

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: um and everything i'm about to go through we've gone through with all of our school leaders at the spring engagement that dr chang uh described so that they were crystal clear about what to tell their teachers, families, students.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: This year, there's no impact whatsoever on graduation requirements.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: There's no proposed changes.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So our current seniors are graduating against the 44 credits and, generally speaking, the five exams to graduate.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: If the Board of Regents votes to adopt the changes that they've discussed, that were just recently discussed at the September meeting, that will decouple the regents from graduation for students who graduate starting next year.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So that's our current juniors and below.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: In addition, there's this move to the one New York State diploma.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Right now, we tend to think of it as a three-level hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Local, which has those exam flexibilities that are primarily used by students with disabilities and some others.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Regents diploma, which is sort of the standard five assessments with scores of 65 or higher.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And the advanced regents, which will still continue to be an option.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: The advanced regents requires students to do a specialized course sequence, some additional regents.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: exams, quite robust.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So that will continue to be an option as an add-on to the one New York State diploma.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So that's for students who graduate starting next year, 2027-28.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: The next real milestone after that is the new transcript, which is targeted for implementation in 2029-30.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: The state will provide standards about how we will need to go about redesigning our transcript.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Our transcript is very standard, course credits, grades, assessment scores.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: But the idea is to show students proficiency in the standards and in the portrait of a graduate and show a much more robust body of evidence.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So that's a few years down the line, 2029, 2029, 30 for implementation.

utterances.text: Chang's advocacy and working with...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So many partners across the city that are very invested philosophically and financially in the success of this work are everyday ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And so as it relates to some of your questions, Jean, if you want to talk a little bit about expansion.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So speaking very specifically to how we are using the community, right, in our bigger ecosystem,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: we've built a really strong employer and workforce ecosystem through the Pathways Advisory Council, which is a sector-based industry commission, school partnerships, and intermediary organizations that connect employers and students.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And so we have what we call a three-legged stool, right?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It's going to be a three-pronged approach.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: One is supporting students directly with funding, training, and technical assistance to develop local employer partnerships and expand work-based learning opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: One of the things that Dr.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Chang has really pushed us on is to really consider, like, what is going on, like, around the corner from our...

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: student schools, where can our students have experiences within community and not just like writ large in larger New York.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So we are going to be doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We also partner with intermediaries such as CareerWise New York to scale the opportunities across industry.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And just to give you an example, today nearly 800 students are participating in youth apprenticeships and we have distributed over $45 million in student wages and stipends through the career connected learning opportunities that we have.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And that's not even including the SYEP wages that we partner with DYCD on.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And then the third piece is just to really create new public sector pathways, including the first of its kind civil service use apprenticeship law, which was passed last winter,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: which is launching this fall with over 100 seniors across 20 city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And that work finally is really strengthened through the close collaboration with DYCD, with DK.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: and the Mayor's Office of Talent and Workforce Development.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Through Career Ready SYEP alone, New York City Public Schools and DYCD provided paid summer work experiences to approximately 23,000 students across 230 high schools.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We're also really trying to figure out how do we couple that with students maybe even earning credit for the work that they're doing over the summer so that they get ahead before they're going to college.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And then in FY25, while Work, Learn, and Grow extends those opportunities into the school year, we're working really closely with Commissioner Escamilla to make sure that we are growing those partnerships.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So as we look at Portrait of a Graduate,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: They're learning, they're getting those attributes, but it's also as scaled as we can possibly get it so that every student has it.

chapters.summary: Joseph thanks the panel and emphasizes equity and support for students. She yields back to the Chair.
chapters.title: Joseph thanks DOE and notes equity concerns before yielding

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Since it's not my hearing, I'm going to stop right there, but I want to say thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Amoy, that always been, you have some great folks working, you know, for DOE, so I'm so grateful.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I have my friend, my super.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Tender here.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Michael Pryor, that's in part of, close to my district, we share a lot.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And I'm a fan of education, you know, whatever you need, whatever I can do.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: So thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Knight.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And equity along the way.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Equity, equity.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member Knight.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks whether a current junior will still need to take Regents exams next year. Katie Hansen says students must still earn 44 credits but there will not be a separate assessment system for graduation, and DOE is telling principals not to let students skip Regents yet.
chapters.title: Dinowitz seeks clarification on transition for current juniors

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just have two questions, and I'll turn it over to Council Member Wong, just about, can you clarify the timeline?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students, I'm a junior now, pretend I'm in high school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm a 21 Jump Street going into...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No one gets the reference.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The old people do, and this one young person does.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You're old enough for me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But Google it.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: I was going to say, it's a younger reference for me, but go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I'll pretend I'm a junior, the oldest looking junior in high school you'll ever meet.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Next year, the portrait is being implemented.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I took all these regents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do I still get to graduate high school, or do I now have to start doing capstone projects and portfolios?

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: No, there's, we're not expected next year to stand up a sort of a one-for-one replacement for the regions exams.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Our understanding, and as you know, these are proposed, not even yet proposed regulations, but our understanding is what the decoupling means is students must pass their 44 credits to graduate.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And within that, of course, there's many ways they're showing their learning in order to earn the credit.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: But there won't be a separate system of assessments or whatever the case may be that students have to complete to meet graduation requirements.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So you're telling me if I'm a junior right now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And my teacher tells me, you got to take the Algebra 2 Regents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to tell him, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: I mean, we've been very clear in our messaging to principals.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: We meet with our point people from the superintendents teams weekly to reinforce.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Nothing has been even proposed, much less adopted by the Board of Regents.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And we don't want a single.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: student to be impacted by saying, oh, I don't have to take my regents.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: But you raise a good point about the transition.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I think the concern is what I said in my opening, which is, you know, without a replacement

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: of equal or more rigor, it's going to turn into, well, I checklist got my 44 credits or the DUE or superintendents might say we're getting pressure to increase graduation rates.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So just do whatever you can to pass the kid.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Things that I've seen in the classroom.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes that schools near City Hall have industry and government access, while other schools are near a safe injection site or men's shelter. He says equity must account for unequal access to partners and opportunities.
chapters.title: Dinowitz warns about equity in work-based learning access across neighborhoods

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just one other comment, just something to be very aware of that principals have brought up to me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like if you go to a high school around here and you mentioned, you know, leveraging local community.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, you're around City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You're around the World Trade Center.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like there's all like in those two places alone, there's a lot of industry and government access.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I was at an outward bound school last year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know what's around the corner from them?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A safe injection site.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is there another school in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know what's around the corner from them?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's like a single adult men's shelter.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That is what is around other schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So as we use the words equity, I want us to remember that certain neighborhoods don't have the same access to industry and government and everything else that others do.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about high chronic absenteeism rates and what DOE is doing to get students to school. Giunta describes attendance teams, school avoidance liaisons, and root-cause work with families, but says she does not have attendance data at hand.
chapters.title: Council Member Wong asks about chronic absenteeism and Portrait readiness

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to turn it over to my friend and colleague, Councilmember Wong.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Who keeps track of a student attendance?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Raise your hand.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My first question to the panel.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You ought to.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Here's my question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: First question.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: It's very disturbing for me to see that such high rates of chronic absenteeism.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And this concerns me because COVID is over many, many years ago.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then we're looking at numbers that are...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: That are far higher than the figures I've seen during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And when you say portrait of a student, portrait of a graduate, you know, that's the first thing come to my mind.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You know, do they go, do they show up for school?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What is being done on that?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because I find that we're not doing enough to get kids to go to school.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Anybody?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah, sure.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'll jump in just to say all of this matters the most when we have our children in school with us for so many reasons.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Deputy Chancellor Flavia Puello-Perdomo helps lead attendance and addressing chronic absenteeism.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: All of our districts have attendance leads, and we have in our schools designated folks that help.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Keep a real practices, attendance teams.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have now the school avoidance liaisons.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: started this year.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have many structures in our schools to connect closely with families, to help get at

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: some of the root causes of what's keeping our children out of school, and helping support families to, to the extent possible, remediate any challenges of getting children to school.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In partnership with them.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So do you have a theory on these high, high chronic absenteeism figures?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think the theory for our chronic absenteeism is multifaceted.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think it is around...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So just a wide variety of different criteria, such as, you know, we have.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So it will take a while to analyze the reasons.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Well, we have.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We have.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I just don't have our attendance data with us right now.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I'll follow up with this.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Wong cites EdTrust New York testimony that schools still do not know how to measure proficiency for current high school students. Giunta says DOE is about to begin broader community engagement and is relying on principals, CECs, and parent leadership structures to share information.
chapters.title: Wong asks what DOE has communicated to students and families about the transition

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I want to expand, Chad, you know, with question on community engagement regarding this.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Portrait.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: At the September 14th Regents meeting, the Ed Trust New York testified that schools still do not know how they will measure proficiency in core subjects for current high school students, even though

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: the proposed changes would affect students currently in grades 9 to 11 in less than a year.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Regent Hassani Prats asks, what resources exist for parents?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: and students in this purgatory period.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question for you is, what has DOE communicated to students and families about this transition?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we are exactly at that point where we're going to be doing much broader community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: There has been a lot of getting us ready at the central level, getting our district teams and leadership ready and our principals.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are counting on our principals and our superintendents.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: They have started engaging their communities at their local CEC meetings.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: district, their DPAC meetings.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We are talking about it now in our parent leadership structures, but our principals working with their school leadership teams as a great

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: and important entry point into explaining what this policy is going, is shaping up to be.

chapters.summary: Wong asks who will take Regents if they are not getting a Regents diploma. Katie Hansen says Regents will still be administered and remain part of the advanced Regents diploma and seals or endorsements like civic readiness and biliteracy.
chapters.title: Wong asks who will take Regents exams if not required for diploma

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So who's going to take the regents if they're not getting a regent's diploma?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Let's say I'm graduating next June.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm going to bring in Katie to come back into some of the academic policy aspects of your questions.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So the regents are still going to be administered.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And as I was alluding to before, the regents are still a component of...

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: The advanced regents diploma, which is still an option available to all of our students.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And they're also a component of many of our seals or endorsements.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So for example, we have a seal of civic readiness, we have a seal of biliteracy, and a few others.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: And for those, students have to do a very robust course sequence, as well as attain certain

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: proficiency on Regents exams and do other expanded learning experiences, sometimes work-based learning, in order to earn those special designations.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So the Regents do still serve that purpose.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: They're one of many measures that students can use to show what they know and can do.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if a CTE-endorsed diploma will become a CTE seal. Hansen says seal and endorsement are synonyms, CTE remains a sticker on the diploma, and no new seals have been created yet by the state.
chapters.title: Wong asks how CTE endorsements will change under new seal structure

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, I have a little time left.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I want to move on to career and technical education, CTE.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: NISAT's timeline calls for redefined SEALs and endorsements in the 2027-28 school year, and the advanced designation is to become a SEAL or endorsement rather than a diploma type.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is, what does DOE understand that would change the CTE students?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Will a CTE-endorsed diploma become a CTE seal?

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So we use seal and endorsement as synonyms.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: It's quite literally a sticker on the diploma, and it would remain.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: CTE, alongside all the others I just named, would remain as a seal or sticker that is affixed to students'diplomas.

chapters.summary: Wong says counselors do not know how to program students toward seals under the new structure. Hansen says existing academic policy resources provide guidance for current programs and DOE will turn key any new state guidance when it becomes available.
chapters.title: Wong asks what guidance counselors have received on programming students toward seals

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Committee staff have learned from school leaders that counselors do not know how to program students towards SEALs under the new structure.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So what guidance has DOE issued to school counselors, and when will more be issued?

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: Yeah, so we already have guidance in our academic policy resources and other materials that we provide to participating schools about what those programs are.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: requirements are for schools who offer those options.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: So just to be clear, there's no, per the September Board of Regents update, there's no new seals yet.

utterances.speaker: Katie Hansen
utterances.text: If the state decides to create new seals, we would then turn key that guidance to our school leaders, our counselors through citywide guidance.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says dozens of principals he has spoken with do not know what to do beyond saying their school has CTE or seal programs. Giunta acknowledges there is ambiguity while state guidance evolves and says DOE is socializing the four transformations and six attributes.
chapters.title: Dinowitz says principals lack information and asks for concrete examples

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Say hello.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I got to say, you use the phrase like the principals are sharing with, you know, their, I guess, SLTs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't know if you use that phrase, but principals are sharing with SLTs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I got to tell you, I've spoken to dozens upon dozens of principals.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: None of them know.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like what they're doing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They have ideas.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They have, well, we're a CTE school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have CTE programs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I think we're well positioned.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We offer the seal of civic readiness.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I think we have that element, but they don't have information to share.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So can you share some of the conversations that you think principals are having or that you know principals are having with what this portrait actually looks like?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think when we're talking about the work that we've done with our principals has been around what is this, what does this mean, what is the timeline, and really making sure that that is what is getting out.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The questions you're asking will go back to your opening statement about like practice.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: in the classroom, what has to change right now.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is, you know, we are partnering so closely with the state on what their next iteration of resources and guidance will be so that we can make sure that we are in full alignment.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: In the meantime, we have these great examples across our system from Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Chang's old district.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And especially Superintendent Prayer, who sat not only on the Blue Ribbon Commission, but is bringing this to life amongst his schools.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I would be surprised if you're hearing from his principals, but I don't want to be naive and say that every single one of our principals has the depth of knowledge of what needs to change or not and when.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is what we're working, we are focused with them right now on socializing what the four transformations are, what the six attributes are, what they need to know for this year,

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: what is up next that will guide where we are going next that they will then need to know.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So there is a space right now that I think there is a little ambiguity because we are watching this process evolve.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But we know that where we want to really lean into is around our SEALs, around our endorsements, around the opportunity to demonstrate knowledge, especially leaning into the performance-based assessments that Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Chang is an expert on.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Would you like to add any more color to that?

chapters.summary: Cheng says principals should be thinking about designing rigorous learning opportunities. Dinowitz pushes back that schools need structure and standardized rubrics, and Cheng brings up Superintendent Michael Prayor to give concrete examples.
chapters.title: Alan Cheng and Superintendent Prayor discuss what schools can do now

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And, and,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Superintendent Prayer, if you'll get ready for the jump seat, we'll get you to sort of be ready to talk a little bit about your own examples.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think, you know, to this question, which is really, what is it that schools can and should be doing right now?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And what is it that the principals are thinking?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And when you say...

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: These principals are saying, I've got this idea.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: This is what I'm thinking about.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think that is where we want them to be.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And schools must be thinking about designing those rigorous learning opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But how do they design them?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to push back.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think there's a lot of ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't think there's a little ambiguity.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like, how are they supposed to know they can work for a year on a portfolio and the Dewey can come back later and say, well, that's not portfolio based assessment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is what is that?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, they need some sort of guidance, some sort of structure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And, you know, we I love that schools are going to have more autonomy and like reflect their communities.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But to some degree, it goes back to the to the standards.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like there has to be some rubric or something that is standardized so principals have a direction in which they can and should go and teachers have a direction.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're talking about something that's going to start in a year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And there's, to my knowledge, no professional development on what this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: looks like and how teachers should be shifting their practice.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like that's what we're...

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think I want to highlight that the New York State standards themselves are not going anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And many of our courses do not result or culminate in Regents examinations.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so this idea that our teachers, our principals have practices in place that already involve multiple measures that allows us to be able to say, what are rigorous demonstrations of what that learning looks like?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And sometimes it is through a project.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Sometimes it's through an oral defense.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Sometimes it's deeply connected to a college course that they are taking.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Those are all different ways that are already in place.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so when principals are saying, hey, look, I've got this idea of how much more I can do, we want to be able to leverage that and continue to be able to work with them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I know you know this, the superintendents go into schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I've been in the schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They say, show me your ELA regions, show me your Algebra 1 regions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's it.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Yeah, I will say that in addition to asking for that information, because that is absolutely crucial and is part of the core foundation of that learning.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We're also asking our superintendents to be able to go into the classroom to say, what are other rigorous forms of demonstration of that learning?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Where are students deeply engaged, having an ownership of that particular?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: their project and where is that going?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And we want to make sure that we have these systems where across superintendencies, they're able to learn from each other and really collaborate across those schools.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so I'm going to use this chance to be able to give Michael an opportunity to say a little bit more about what does it look like?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Because I really want to be able to push on this notion that

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Schools have opportunities to learn deeply from each other.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Students are informing and guiding this process along the way, which I think is absolutely crucial.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And all of this is building towards a higher set of expectations because we know that these multiple measures really...

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Are able to have shared expectations, common rubrics and guidelines, the very things that you've talked about that we need to make sure that we continue to be able to do with schools.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz administers the affirmation to Michael Prayor, superintendent of Brooklyn South High Schools, and asks him to describe what Portrait-aligned learning actually looks like in schools.
chapters.title: Dinowitz swears in Superintendent Michael Prayor and asks for classroom examples

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, which I, and I want to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think I'll have to swear you in too, but I want to hear, and I want to hear like what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Cause we can talk about like the idea of good assessment, but it's really important that what hasn't been spoken about, I think to so many of our teachers and principals is just like what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And any teacher knows they go to the PD.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I've gotten the PD on like the project-based learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And, you know, all the time they ask, okay, so I still need to get my kids to pass the regents.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like, how does this relate to the regents?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like, we're measured on something.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students are measured on something.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Schools are measured on something.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we have to.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: to know what that something looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And as much as I, my feelings on the regents, at least we know what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So that's, so if you could help elucidate that, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm just going to, if you raise your right hand, do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth before this council?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In your testimony?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Michael Pereira, superintendent of Brooklyn South High Schools.

chapters.summary: Prayor, who served on the Blue Ribbon Commission, describes HEAT (Healthcare, Energy, Education, Agriculture, Technology), a place-based program with partners like the Federal Reserve Bank, Cisco, and Maimonides Hospital. Students research real problems and defend proposals before experts.
chapters.title: Superintendent Prayor describes Brooklyn South HEAT program and place-based learning

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: So I'm going to just say welcome to Brooklyn South as I share what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: So I had the pleasure of sitting on the Blue Ribbon Commission, and there gave me a lot of insight to what we were doing correctly, some gaps.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And some things that I needed to improve on in Brooklyn South and take advantage of the opportunity having sat and heard from a lot of constituents, but mostly students.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Students were able to share exactly what they felt was missing and yet what they desired to have.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And hence, was the development of a program called HEAT.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And HEAT stands for Healthcare, Energy, Education, Agriculture, and Technology.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: It's a place-based learning program.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: It creates sustained learning experiences connected to rigorous academic work with professional, civic, and historical context.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And I do want to say for the record, I want to say they're not here, but council members, Joseph,

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Narcisse for helping me find partners like Con Edison, Mamani's Hospital, and a few others.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: I just want to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: So what is HEAT?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And I'm going to give you some clear examples of what students are doing.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: At the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, right around the corner, students travel from Brooklyn to the Federal Reserve Bank.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: At the bank, students study economics and investigate how markets, government, and individuals shape the flow of money and resources.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They examine a societal issue through an economic lens, work with professional economists, conduct research, produce a well-researched proposal, and defend it before economists and experts.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They are there for the whole year.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They travel in a cohort between 18 to 25 students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sorry, this is an individual school?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: This is a collaboration of schools across Brooklyn South.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, so 18 to 25 kids throughout Brooklyn South.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And that's just one.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: At Cisco is another one.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: At Cisco, students study cybersecurity and investigate industry-specific cybersecurity challenges.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Working with professionals, students analyze evolving challenges, develop solutions within incident response protocols for a particular audience, and present and defend those solutions before technology experts.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Students have to understand the content, analyze an authentic problem, design a solution, and defend their reasoning.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: At Momani's Hospital, students explore areas including women's health,

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: surgery for women's health, general surgery, pathology and radiology.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They work with medical professions, investigate pressing issues, conduct research, develop a proposed solution, and defend their work before medical experts who probe their reasoning.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: The evidence isn't that the students spent time in a hospital.

chapters.summary: Prayor says students study the Freedom Riders and travel south, study Poland and Holocaust survivor testimony, and examine Barbados and the transatlantic slave trade. They produce research papers, documentaries, and civic action projects defended before panels.
chapters.title: Prayor describes global citizenship projects including Freedom Riders, Poland, and Barbados

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: The evidence is what the students researched, reasoned, produced, communicated, and defended.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Then there's traveling, because one of the attributes is global citizenship.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: I just want to share a little bit about what students are learning.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Students study the Freedom Riders, and if anybody remember the Freedom Riders.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They analyze historical documents, primary resources, oral histories, and examine contemporary connections to civic activism.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They produce a scholarly research paper, a civic action project addressing a contemporary injustice, and a public presentation that defend

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: before educators, peers, community members, and civic leaders.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: We're not simply labeling the student as a global citizen.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: We're examining what the student actually did and produced.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And so those students trace the footsteps of the Freedom Riders, and they travel for two weeks across down south.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Then I want to talk about Poland.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And Poland is very important also.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: The students studying Poland, they analyze historical documents and survivor testimony, work with Holocaust survivors, and extend the inquiry through place-based learning at Holocaust sites in Poland.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They produce documentaries and civic action projects and present and defend their work.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They actually get to...

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Interview living survivors and then produce a documentary in this course.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Travel is not the product.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Learning is the product.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Place becomes part of the text.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And then lastly, I would just share students studying Barbados in the transatlantic slave trade and its impact on the African diaspora, analyzing primary resources, historical texts, oral histories, cultural narratives,

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: and historical records.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They produced a scholarly research paper in a collaborative civic action project

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: addressing contemporary questions of justice, power, inequality, and defend their work at the civic showcases in June.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: The experience creates the context, the academic work provides the experience, and those students also travel in a cohort all throughout Brooklyn South.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: For two weeks, they study abroad, and that becomes an alignment to approach a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Thank you, Superintendent Pereira.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I want to highlight that these are things that a given school may not be able to have the resources or the planning to be able to execute on their own, but through the great work of our students,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: superintendents, we're beginning to be able to create opportunities, curriculum, and work that we can share across schools.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And that this is happening truly, you know, I would love to be able to have more of our high school superintendents and our community superintendents up here talking about that.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: It is also...

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Yeah, we're all working today.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: But it is also important to be able to highlight that just because a school may be geographically located in one part of our city,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: you see here the examples where we're able to bring them and leveraging the entire resources of our city, as well as some of the amazing networks and resources across our country and our world.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks about assessment criteria and whether rubrics go through DOE. Prayor says rubrics are teacher-created using standards and reviewed with academic policy, and Dinowitz confirms they are approved by DOE Central.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks how HEAT rubrics are developed and whether DOE Central approves them

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate those examples.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Did you develop, now in terms of assessment, right, maintaining the rigor.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: One, those are all high schoolers who are doing this?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Yes, 11th graders and 12th graders.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: 11Th graders.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how are the rubrics?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or the assessment criteria developed, are those approved by you?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are those approved or reviewed or audited by the DOE Central?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Yes, we do work with academic policy.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Also, they're teacher-created.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: We use the standards, of course.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: And then the assessments is what they publish, what the students actually do to show that they demonstrated the learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But let's, because now we're talking about, you know, the students in Brooklyn South held to the same rigorous standards as students in the Bronx, Queens, wherever.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so I just, I, I, I,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to make sure it's a yes that whatever rubric is being used to assess the rigor of those assignments and experiences, they go through the DOE and are approved by DOE Central.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: I would say yes, because that's what we do.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: They work closely with us.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So that's great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's great.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks how many students engage in these programs. Prayor says about 400 11th graders participate, but Brooklyn South has about 31,000 high schoolers and roughly 10,000 11th graders. Dinowitz notes the scale challenge.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks about scale of Prayor's programs versus Brooklyn South enrollment

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So now I need to ask about scale.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many students total did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You talked about 18 to 25 for the first one.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just like in total, how many students?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Engage in these types of projects?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: So we have, each year we have about 411 graders.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Some of those 11 graders, once they go through the program, they become seniors and they become mentors for the new 11 graders.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But let me ask you, every single...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: 11Th grader in Brooklyn South goes to this program.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You're saying it's about 400?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: About 400.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And how many 11th graders total are there in Brooklyn South?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: I probably have about, I would say...

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: I have 31,000 students.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: So 11th grade is...

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Maybe about 10,000.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: About 10,000.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You said 31,000 high schoolers?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: I have 31,000 high schools.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So probably a little more than if it's quarter, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's probably a little less than 10,000, but fine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Whatever.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's like 7,500, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So now we have the issue, one of the other issues that came up about scale.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I appreciate those examples.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Chang, you have a lot of examples from your portfolio-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have this issue of scale.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Great things going on in our school.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's clear, according to your testimony, the rubrics are assessed by something central in the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, that has to be expanded to about 7,000 more students in your district alone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is the plan for that?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks how DOE will expand these opportunities to every 11th grader. Cheng says DOE is working with superintendents to share practices, leverage existing programs like seals, CTE, and portfolios, and use report cards and transcripts to recognize rigor.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE for plan to scale Portrait-aligned assessments to all students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How does the DOE go into support in expanding these types of opportunities to every single 11th grader who has to complete a project or an assessment like this?

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: Well, again, there are other programs that the students are involved in.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: There's CTE programs they have.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: We have the Brooklyn STEAM Center.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: There are other programs students are involved in.

utterances.speaker: Michael Prayor
utterances.text: These are students who might not be involved in one of those other programs that have an opportunity to apply and be selected for what we're offering.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So broadly, what is the plan to scale?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Maybe some here are CTE.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Maybe some here are these 411th graders.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But is every single student currently engaged in a portrait of the graduate-esque assignment for each of their classes?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I think as part of this multi-year initiative, we are working closely with our superintendents, our principals, to be able to create additional opportunities where they're able to learn from other schools,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: as well as making sure that the existing opportunities that they have, for example, the seal of civic readiness, the seal of bi-literacy, our career and technical education programs, our higher education offerings and partnerships, our summer youth employments,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: our portfolios and panels, right?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So there is a wide collection of this work.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We want to make sure, one, that every single one of our schools from K all the way through 12 understand deeply what else exists out there.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And we know our principals and our teachers are eager to be able to learn.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So one part of the scaling is ensuring a greater understanding of the existing strengths and assets that we already have.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: A second thing is really making sure that superintendents are providing their leadership to their schools to do an asset mapping of what is it across our network of schools that we can help support and build out.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And then finally, we want to be able to recognize the higher achievements and the rigor by virtue of student report cards and transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And I think that is an additional way for us to be able to communicate to families, this is the set of expectations that we are providing and how they're able to read.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: those expectations.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says the Portrait starts in 2027-28, teachers and principals need training and direction, and asks about structural supports. He also plugs the upcoming civics hearing and Seal of Civic Readiness.
chapters.title: Dinowitz reiterates need for teacher training and principal guidance before 2027

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to reiterate that if this is starting in the 27-28 school year, the portrait, again, we have a school year that's going to start in less than a year.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Teachers need to be trained.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Principals need to know what they're doing without this sort of stuff.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to ask about leveraging your assets, but I

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you want to make a plug?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that next month we are having a hearing along with the Committee on Higher Education specifically on civics in our schools, including the Seal of Civic Readiness.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What's that?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're excited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You're excited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm excited.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: First Deputy Chancellor, you'll probably be there too.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That was, I said we see you every week.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I do want to plug also, or just remind everyone that I think two years ago when I was chair of higher ed, we had a hearing on the seal of biliteracy.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And after that, CUNY started giving college credit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For students who successfully completed the seal and had it on their report card.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I say all that, one, to say that this council stands ready to work in partnership with you on these seals, and that we've done it, and I, as a council member and chair, believe in them as what it could bring to the table.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now that, yeah.

chapters.summary: Cheng clarifies that state requirements for measuring and monitoring Portrait proficiencies take effect in 2029, not 2027. He says DOE wants to be ahead of the curve and already has examples.
chapters.title: Alan Cheng clarifies state monitoring requirements do not begin until 2029

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Chair, I also want to just use this opportunity to provide some additional clarity for you and for our families out there, which is that this particular transition, I hear you use the year 2027.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: State requirement with regards to measuring and monitoring progress towards these portrait of a graduate proficiencies do not take effect until the year 2029.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so we are committed to and want to be ahead of the curve and already

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: have some great examples, but wanted to be able to clarify a little bit of that timeline, which is not that all of a sudden in the year 2027, we would have these new requirements.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says communication between DOE, principals, teachers, and families needs work. He asks if DOE has completed asset mapping. Cheng says DOE has a robust sense of existing practices including Future Ready, affinity partners, and consortium schools.
chapters.title: Dinowitz says communication needs work and asks if asset mapping is complete

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think the communication between you guys, the principals, the teachers, the families needs a lot of work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the reason I say that is because

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I have lists of pages and pages of notes from the various groups of principals that I've met with.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And they don't know a lot of what seems to be the basic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Even though you've gone over the timeline with them, I think the same basic question of what it looks like in practice is not answered.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to ask about the assets.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: At this point in the year, it seems to me that the asset mapping should have been done.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is your asset mapping of all your schools done?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or are you continually, is that ongoing?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So what we do have is that we have a robust sense of the landscape of the different kinds of practices that our schools are already doing.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I know you don't want me to repeat all the different ways that this work is already happening.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We have our 190 future-ready NYC schools.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We have 150-plus schools that are part of one of our affinity partnerships that have been doing this work.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We've got our consortium schools that are in our network.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So that is one key.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: part of the asset mapping.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I do think we also want to make sure that we're taking into consideration what is the size of the school, what is the teacher capacity, and how we can work with that particular community and that need to be able to help support them.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what structure exists for principals and teachers from non-portfolio schools to visit consortium schools and how many intervisitations have been done. Giunta says the old program is not currently stood up but visits have occurred.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks how many intervisitations have occurred between Regents and portfolio schools

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Schools,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know this from the teacher perspective.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When I was a model teacher and peer collaborative teacher, we got, you know, I think the school got extra money.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We got extra money.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And part of that program was to do intervisitations.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'd visit other schools and bring best practices back to the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many intervisitations have been done between these non-port, these regents schools and the portfolio-based, the consortium schools?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So that is a practice where we've had in years past, whether there was under a showcase schools, lighthouse schools model or learning partner.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No, I know it's done.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I just want to be like, get really to it, which is, I guess, April is when you got the positions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We knew the portrait was coming beforehand.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You've said time and again correctly that we have schools doing great things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The superintendent highlighted a number of good things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What is the structure that's in place to get, you know, principals and like, you know, certain teachers?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: From schools that don't do portfolio-based assessments to visit the schools that do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What does that structure look like and how many intervisitations have been done between those schools?

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: The program that you were in, I learned something new about you every time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'll give you one more when we're done here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But the regions.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We don't have that program currently stood up.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: It is a structure that we have been talking about, especially as we want to scale up.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Examples and models for our educators to learn from so they can replicate.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I would say in my former role where I was leading the professional learning for superintendents and their teams, even before the transition, we were jumping into the portrait of a graduate work.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Part of our professional learning plan with our superintendents, specifically more so at the high school level, was intervisitations, even as part of the culture of our school.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
