utterances.text: So I don't think I would have to go back to our agendas and look at how many schools, but like...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Superintendent prayer hosted a visit all of his i think almost every high school superintendent over the last few years have been hosting visits and highlighting these practices in the high school world especially as it relates to portrait of a graduate

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: with undergirding of like how are you implementing solves how are you implementing reads that's where we have concentrated our community superintendents but i think even um before the transition into these new positions it was the

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: February superintendent meeting, we were at Lincoln Center.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I remember it specifically because Superintendent Preyer, then Superintendent Dr.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Chang, and some of our community superintendents did a panel discussion for their colleagues around how they were thinking about what...

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: What exists in their district and how they're moving it into the conversation of New York Inspires and Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it seems to me it has to, you know, again, you know, what does it look like?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think it has to look like structural supports from the top.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I don't mean just directives.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, schools need funding to do this.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: They need, you know, whether it's coverage for teachers, support for professional development.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And by the way, so.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: for the consortium schools who are going to be taking time out of their schedules and conducting, whether it's formal or informal PD, the structural support and the financial support to our schools to dig into this work.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says schools need funding, coverage for teachers, and support for professional development. He says consortium schools should be compensated for hosting and training, and DOE should commit resources and structure.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls for structural and financial support for teacher and principal training

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's work that, so far as I understand, principals and teachers...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Want to do, they want to be engaged with, they don't want to be left figuring it out for themselves.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we have, as you've pointed to time and again, a wealth of knowledge in our city of how to start approaching this portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think you just kind of have to take a leap and do it and commit the resources and the time and the structure to doing it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Wong has more questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to turn it back to him if he's ready.

chapters.summary: Wong says CEC members and citywide councils have not been engaged in the process. Giunta says DOE is entering the next step of local CEC conversations and welcomes Sharon Rensher to describe prior outreach.
chapters.title: Wong asks how CECs and families are engaged in implementation planning

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, I served in my school board for four years, and I still talk to the current CEC members regularly, and also citywide council and high schools.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I talk to them regularly, but I don't think anybody there has...

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Has engaged in this process.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So my question for you is, how are you approaching them?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: How are they being engaged in implementation planning?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And do you have a feedback mechanism exist for the families to wade in on local implementation decisions?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Please answer.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I'm going to welcome Sharon Rensher in, who does our state partnerships, to talk about a lot of the outreach to date.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But I do want to acknowledge that that is exactly the moment we're in for our next step, is having more regular conversations at our local CEC meetings, but also, you know, the Chancellor and I and the Cabinet meet with our CEC presidents.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We used to join those also once a month.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And really making sure all of our structures, that this is a more prevalent conversation.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: That is on tap and ready to go.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But there has been a tremendous amount of engagement that Sharon Renter has been a part of, especially in partnership with the state.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So I just want to give her the opportunity to just share a little bit about that.

chapters.summary: Rensher, Senior Executive Director for State and Federal Education Policy, describes NYCPS representation on the Blue Ribbon Commission, borough stakeholder meetings in 2020-2021, and student feedback that Regents prep took time away from projects, internships, and creative work.
chapters.title: Sharon Rensher describes stakeholder engagement and student feedback on Regents

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: Thank you, First Deputy Chancellor, and good afternoon, Chair Dinnowitz, and of course, Committee Member Wong, and also all of the colleagues who are not here to share this information with.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: My name is Sharon Rensher.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: I'm Senior Executive Director for State and Federal Education Policy and Planning on the FDC's team.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: We use FDC, you know, that's First Deputy Chancellor.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: We like calling her FDC.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And again, thank you for the opportunity to appear before you today.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: So as our FTC has shared, we come before you not only as implementers of a state policy, but as genuine believers in this, in what New York City Inspires can accomplish.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And as we've continued to describe, of course, what NYCPS is going and where we're going with NY Inspires, just to share with you a little bit of what we've done so far, how we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: We've been engaged with our stakeholders in this process.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: So as FTC shared after Commissioner Betty Rosa did initiate this conversation

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: and establish the Blue Ribbon Commission, we did have 10 members who served on the Blue Ribbon Commission, and that included not only our teachers and our parents and our students, our community members.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: There were actually 10 members that actually represented us, of course.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: After the Blue Ribbon Commission, we did, or as it was established, we held in 2020 and 2021 stakeholder engagement meetings across our city and every borough.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: We actually had two in every borough, and they were well represented by all of our stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And, of course, we heard from our stakeholders, but particularly from our students.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And I'll share with you some of what our students have shared, as well as just talk to you about some of the engagement that happened after that.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: Both current and high school students and recent graduates.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And you probably heard this as well, and we have students who are represented here who probably could share some of their same thoughts.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: But they shared very clearly strong opinions with clarity, with passion.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: They told us that the amount of time devoted to Regents exam prep during their high school years was excessive.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: They described it as time taken away from learning, from the projects, the internships, the community experiences, the creative and collaborative work that they've done.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: believed would have actually prepared them for college and for careers.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And the recent graduates were particularly direct about the gap they had experienced.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: They arrived at the CUNY and SUNY colleges having spent years practicing passing tests and found that college expected something very different from them.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: They expected

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: independent research, analytical writing across disciplines, collaborative problem solving, creative and critical thinking across ambiguous open-ended challenges.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: These were the skills their professors expected from them from day one, and these were precisely the skills that their high school experiences had given them the least time to develop, and now New York Inspires will give us the opportunity to support them with those.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: So not only was New York City Public Schools present in the community engagement process and directly represented on the Blue Ribbon Commission, we then held ambassador stakeholder meetings in every borough

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: to share back, and actually were the commission members or commission representatives who actually conducted these ambassador stakeholder meetings in every community.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And we did, again, hear from our parents, from our teachers, from our school administrators and our students what they would like us to see and how they would like to be further engaged.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And this is now the opportunity for us to actually engage them further.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: I will share with you that we are very much engaged, continually engaged in structures across the state.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: both with the state and with our partners at the Big Five districts and our BOCES partners across the state as we're thinking about and strategically planning, and we also have robust stakeholder

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: representation in those conversations.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: And that will lead us, again, to further develop how we're going to engage our stakeholders going forward.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if DOE will ensure research is a central element in portfolio assessments. Alan Cheng answers yes. Dinowitz notes that was the easiest answer he has received.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks whether DOE will require research as a key assessed component

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You mentioned one example of students entering CUNY, entering college, not prepared with many of the skills.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are you assessing what skills need to be...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Assessed or taught more rigorously.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You mentioned research, for example.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Obviously, the Regis doesn't test it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so a teacher's or school's disincentivized from investing in that sort of education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is it the DOE's plan then to ensure that in any of their portfolios, there's a significant amount of research done?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because like I said, if you're assessing it, it's going to get that investment of time and money.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: I think Superintendent Pratt shared in the models that he described the amount of research that students were expected to engage in as part of the projects that they were engaged in with the partners.

utterances.speaker: Sharon Rensher
utterances.text: So absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, but I just want to make sure it is the DOE's central director.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For a goal, not the will of a very good superintendent, which I said on the record, sir.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know your first answer.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All of our superintendents are good.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But after that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Amazing.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Say that question one more time for me.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, the fact that certain skills exist as being assessed in these portfolio-based assessments is different than the DEWE making a decision

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that research has to be an integral component in a certain number of the projects.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So my question is, you mentioned research as, I'm using it as an example of one of the elements colleges say many high schoolers are ill-prepared for in college.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is it then the DOE's intention when they are reviewing rubrics to ensure that research is a key component, that that is actually being assessed and measured?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what level—school, superintendent, or central—will review rubrics. Cheng outlines the sequence: state standards, DOE academic guidelines, curriculum team quality review, and backward mapping from Portrait competencies.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks what structure DOE will use to review rubrics for rigor citywide

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just, that was the easiest answer you ever got.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I just want to make sure, certain schools report that in the past, rubrics were submitted to the state for a rigor review.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: What structure does the DOE anticipate?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And at what level, school superintendent central, for ensuring the rigor?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I heard you say you review his rubrics for the portfolio-based assessment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Your goal is to review all of the rubrics across the city centrally?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So I think I want to outline sort of the sequence of things and the system that has to be in place.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: The state education department sets out the state standards.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And for a long time, they've set an exit exam for specific courses.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: But you know what we will do here in the city is to be able to work with our Office of Policy and Evaluation.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We lay out really clear academic guidelines.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We have our curriculum and teaching team that works with our teachers and our schools to be able to assess the quality of each of the content.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And within that, what we're layering on is that as part of this transition, the state has said across our portrait of our graduate competencies, these are specific.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Proficiencies that are critical for students to be able to find ways of mastering over time.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And so what we're excited about doing is to be able to work collaboratively with our schools to be able to say, once that language that the state is able to put out,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And then we can then begin to backwards map and say, well, what is the progression for us to be able to get there?

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We know that this does not only occur in high school.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We need to be able to develop research skills in elementary schools as well as middle school.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: That then results in a set of standards and progressions that is tailored to each of our grade bands.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: From there, we will work collectively with our schools to provide the...

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: necessary training and norming around what are the different ways that students can use to be able to demonstrate mastery of that particular skill over time.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says DOE is the largest district and should be vocal about what guidance should look like, citing youth journalism as an example. Cheng says DOE is taking leadership and leveraging existing strengths and student voices.
chapters.title: Dinowitz urges DOE to lead rather than wait for state guidance

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The DEU is the largest school district in the country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And what I'm hearing is

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, a lot from that answer is, well, let's wait and see what the state tells us.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that that may be, you know, a perception that may be out there.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And I want to use the opportunity to really clarify, as you've heard me say, there are tremendous positive examples of a head start that New York City already has in place.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: For example, and you've heard, and I want to make sure we put on record, that the New York State Performance Standards Consortium

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: has over 30 schools for over 20 years have had a state-recognized set of rubrics and guidelines that are accepted as just as good,

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: oftentimes better examples of what a high-quality bar is that has backed by evidence that is accepted by universities such as CUNY and SUNY system.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And through that process, there is alignment, validation, norming, and scoring that is in place.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: So I do think that the...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I know they exist, but I think as we've discussed, one element is taking the lead internally and saying, look, we know these things are good, setting up those structures to communicate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And to ensure that, like, internally, that principals are communicating with one another.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Again, the support, the structural support and the finances.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But also, as the largest school district, I think it's okay to say, hey, like, we're in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're doing it right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Dear New York State, this is what it should look like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And it just, you know, when I hear like we're waiting for the guidance, you should be really a lot more vocal in what the guidance should look like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, like today alone, we have these youth journalism students who are here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, I know all the work you're doing in the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're funding in the council.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like that's what it could look like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like why not elevate these students and say.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Dear State, it should look like youth journalism, sincerely, the largest school district in the country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that's where I think we kind of, like, we shouldn't be waiting and hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We should be elevating these things.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says teachers have spent careers teaching to tests and will need extensive professional development. He hopes DOE is prepared and raises concerns about affinity contracts and private vendor costs.
chapters.title: Dinowitz emphasizes need for DOE-funded professional development

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Let me make it very clear.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We are not saying we're not doing anything and we're simply waiting.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: We are very much taking the leadership.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: In fact, much of what the state guidance and their hearings and their feedback processes leveraged the existing strengths that we have.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: I also think, as the first deputy chancellor said, this is the right opportunity for us to be able to provide bold leadership with regards to what we believe is possible.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: And a lot of this will be a commitment to communicating.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: to be able to help people see those possibilities by virtue of intervisitations, but it is also leveraging our students, our student journalists, and others to be able to say, this is what we care deeply about.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: These are the ways in which, through civic engagement, we can help shape the future of what is being expected of a New York City public school student.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I know I've spoken a lot about principals and the support for principals and the teachers.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't want it to go unsaid.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The incredible amount of professional development that's going to need to be put into this, professional development that has to be from you guys, financially supported or created or administered by the DOE.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, when a teacher spends their college, sorry, their grad school, the first years, 10, 20 years of their career, teaching for one purpose, which would be great education at the end of the year to test.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's a lot of teaching that needs to go into and a lot of development that needs to go into changing that assessment structure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I hope the DOE is prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I also want to note, I know it's not budget season, but we're always in budget.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It feels like we're always in budget season.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Last school year, or last budget cycle, the affinity contract was under consideration to be cut.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like it was something that we...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: had to fight for to get it restored.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I also noticed in your testimony, you uplifted Affinity as one of these networks that supports this type of learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so can we just commit to not putting the Affinity contract on the table for being cut if that is one of the networks that's supporting this very type of learning that is the future of our school system?

chapters.summary: Dinowitz notes the affinity contract was considered for cuts last budget cycle and asks for a commitment not to cut it. Giunta says DOE is not in budget season but takes the feedback and values affinity partners.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks DOE not to cut affinity contracts supporting Portrait-aligned learning

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: You know, I think last year when we were looking for cost savings across the agency, there was a lot of conversations.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I think what really ended up being at the forefront of the conversation was not necessarily the full affinity contract.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We were looking at all sorts of aspects.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So we are not in that season yet, but I will take your feedback.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: I will take your comment also as feedback.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And we are very, very grateful for our affinity partners and the work that they're doing and we look forward to partnering with them in the scaling of this work because they have a real strength and blueprint

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: of how this can look and the kinds of support our schools will need that aren't directly working with them.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to amend what you said.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it my feedback.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I would call it a supplement to your feedback.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says DOE has a wealth of internal expertise through affinity networks, consortium schools, internationals, and the UFT Teacher Center. He warns against expensive private vendor contracts for training.
chapters.title: Dinowitz urges DOE to rely on internal expertise over private vendors

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A supplement to your feedback.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And on the topic of the budget, the issue of cost savings, one of the things we're looking at in this,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: council are certain contracts, where a lot of the contracts go to the private companies.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I would just tell you, as you've noted numerous times during this hearing and in our private conversations outside of these hearings, we have a wealth of knowledge in our city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have the Affinity Network, we have the consortium schools, the internationals, all of these schools, these teachers, these administrators,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Together, we have a U of T teacher center.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We don't really need to go outside to private vendors and pay them exorbitant fees to teach teachers and principals things we probably already know internally.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And so what I don't want to see is as these years come up, find, you know, a hundred million dollar contract for some private company.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When we could do it much more efficiently, much less money, and much higher quality by leaning on our educators that we have currently in the system.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to Councilmember Wong after...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong.

chapters.summary: Wong asks how personal finance rollout is going and who teaches it. Dowling says schools can use a designated course, embedded instruction, CTE pathway, or combination, and teachers may be social studies, CTE, or math depending on the school model.
chapters.title: Wong asks about personal finance rollout for grades 5-12 and teacher licensure

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have a question concerning the personal finance on the phase two of New York Inspires that was adopted by Board of Regents.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: There's a K-12 personal finance education requirement.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Effective on 2026-27 school year.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: For grades 5 to 12.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then for 2027-28 school year for grades K-4, how has the rollout gone so far?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And then please talk about it.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Oh, great.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: We had Jane speak a little bit before about personal finance, so I'm going to turn it over to her.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And I would say, I'm not sure if we need Delia teed up.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: If she wants to jump in and compliment, she leads our curriculum and instruction work.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And my part two to that is like math teachers teaching it or social studies or somebody else is teaching this.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Sure, Council Member Wong.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We talked a little bit about it at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We did spend a lot of time really teeing up, making sure that our school districts and our superintendents, and particularly our teachers, were really set up to execute

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: starting this fall for the grade bands that you spoke to during our summer institute session where we had 1,600 of our teachers and district champions help to execute.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: What I spoke to earlier is that we have selected five, the implementation right now for grades five through 12 is that we,

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: our schools can provide instruction through a designated course, embedded instruction, a CTE pathway, or a combination of approaches.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And as a result, the implementation may occur.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: During different grades or semesters, during the school's academic program.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: or even, you know, depending on what their scheduling structure looks like.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And as students progress through the grade bands, the instruction is going to become increasingly more difficult and complex, right?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: What you're teaching a fifth grader is going to be different than what you're teaching an 11th grader who's applying to college.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: And we have selected several programs that we have worked with.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: I mentioned EverFi before.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: Another one is NextGen Financial Generation, which is one of the ones that are– I knew that one you would know.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: But what we did was really making sure that we took in the feedback from our schools and because we have been doing financial literacy through the Future Ready program.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So are these finance teachers like math teachers, social studies, or they're special license?

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It depends on how our schools want to actually implement the work.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It could be a social studies teacher.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It could be a CTE teacher.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: It could be a math teacher.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: So we are not designating that.

utterances.speaker: Jane Martínez Dowling
utterances.text: We just really want to make sure, as Chair Dynowitz and I talked about earlier, that the programs that we are using are meeting the standards that the state has set up.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have one follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Wong asks if DOE has begun planning for the climate education requirement effective in 2027-28. Cordelia Veve says DOE is mapping state climate standards into existing science curriculum and will provide guidance to schools.
chapters.title: Wong asks about climate education requirement and curriculum mapping

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: On March of this year, the Board of Regents adopted what's called a climate education requirement,

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: effective in the 2027-28 school year for grades 5 to 12, and for 2028-29 school year for grades K to 4.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: My question is, has DOE begun planning?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: for the climate education rollout and what subject areas and license areas will carry that.

utterances.speaker: Alan Cheng
utterances.text: Katie and Sharon.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Anybody answer that?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think I can take that.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Delia Beve here, Chief of Curriculum and Instruction.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: So I think very similarly to the personal finance rollout, what we're doing is we're taking what the state has said, they've given us clarity around what are those standards for climate education,

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: and then mapping that into curriculum that we already have.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And so what happened for personal finance was they took the finance education that they were already using in CTE and pathways.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: What we're looking at now for the climate education is looking at our science curriculum so that we can very clearly say to schools, right, to speaking to consistency, we can say here's where that lives in the curriculum that you're already using.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: As you make instructional decisions, make sure that you are leaning into these particular units because we know that those hit the climate education standards that the state has set forth for us.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can I pause for one second?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Don't think we swore you in.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: You didn't.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I raised my hand earlier, though.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm just going to do it now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you affirm, tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee, and to respond honestly to Councilmember questions?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Now I do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now you do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Which means, Councilmember Wong, I think you better watch out.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Everything she said before that, maybe not true.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Wong asks what lessons from personal finance apply to climate education. Veve says DOE learned from NYC Reads and Solves that central clarity and guidance plus local flexibility are critical, and that consistency in materials and collaboration matter.
chapters.title: Wong asks lessons learned from personal finance for climate education rollout

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The follow-up, any lessons learned from the personal finance rollout and how would that apply here for the climate education?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: So I think that we can't learn fully from personal finance rollout, right?

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We just started.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: But I do think what we have learned from our large-scale implementation of New York City Reads and New York City Solves is we need clarity and guidance from central.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And then we also need to create the guidance and guardrails for local decisions to be made, whether those decisions are made at the district level or those are made at the school level, and then in some instances also at the classroom level.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And so clarity and guidance from central is really important.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: making sure that we have the materials that are useful, we have the models that we are putting forward, and then we provide the space for people to iterate.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And I just want to say one more thing.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: We've spoken about consistency.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: I think, Chair Denowitz, that's what you've really been hammering on.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: Consistency is about the materials, but it's also about the ways in which we work together.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: And so we're really thinking about what is the role that Central plays in collaborating with districts to make sure they have the guidance, and then what happens at the district level to make sure that the district is creating the space for schools to work together so that they are learning.

utterances.speaker: Cordelia Veve
utterances.text: They're using shared materials, and they're able to take what works in one school and transfer and translate it to another school.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: No, I have no more.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz repeats Veve's phrase 'clarity and guidance from Central' and thanks the panel. He notes this is the biggest change to high school graduation he has seen.
chapters.title: Dinowitz summarizes need for clarity and guidance from central

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Let me just write it down.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Clarity and guidance from Central.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think you said it twice.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Look.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz says this is the biggest change to graduation requirements he has seen. NYC can make it special and rigorous or fail students. He calls for increased communication, guidance, support, and accountability.
chapters.title: Dinowitz says Portrait could be transformative or a failure for students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: There's certainly a lot more.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: On this topic to discuss for sure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This is the biggest change, I think, to high schools and graduation requirements that I've ever seen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we have here the opportunity to turn it into something very special, very rigorous, very meaningful for our students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Or we can go down the road of failing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And if there's one place we shouldn't fail, it's our kids, especially in a system that has so much good experience doing this under your leadership, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Chang, right, and through all the people on the panel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We've discussed a number of things today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Clearly increased communication, increased guidance, clarity and guidance from central, you know, support for the teachers and the principals.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A lot of work that still needs to go into it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to, you know, continue to stay ready to work with you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And also, as always, hold the DOE accountable because we are, again, talking about the future of our city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We're talking about our kids.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And there's nothing that's more important to me than that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So with increased communication, really creating a structure around best practices, providing the

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: teachers and principals actual supports and structures for sharing best practices, figuring out scaling to scale this to the largest school district in the system and lean on the expertise within our system.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think this really can be something truly transformative for our children and for our city.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I want to once again thank you all for coming.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I encourage you to stay to hear from our students, a lot of youth journalism students here who've patiently waited, but who are also going to highlight some of the incredible work that they do.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Giunta thanks the Council for the opportunity to clarify and have a public conversation. She acknowledges DOE must get better at being clear about what it is doing now and next, and calls it a promise on their checklist.
chapters.title: Giunta thanks Council and promises better communication

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: Thank you so much for the opportunity to add some clarity, have a more public conversation about it, and also know, like, we need to get better at being very clear about what we're doing now and next.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: And that is a promise that is on our checklist.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: But it really is wonderful to have the conversation today.

utterances.speaker: Danielle Giunta
utterances.text: So thank you for it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz opens public testimony, reminds the public to remain silent, says the witness table is reserved for testifiers, and prohibits video recording from the table. He sets two minutes per speaker, says students go first, and explains how to submit written testimony.
chapters.title: Dinowitz opens public testimony and reads rules

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right, first panel, public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If I don't read my script, just so you know, I feel like the meeting becomes illegal.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We have to do the whole thing over again.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I now open the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance slip with a sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If someone could please close the door in the back, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight topic.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you are a student, please write student prominently near the top of your appearance slip.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We will do our best to accommodate you and allow you to provide your testimony as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit to the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may also...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Email written testimony to testimony at council.mrc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I will now call the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are you excited?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are you excited?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Seems a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No one wants to be the first panel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You want to be the first panelist.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Are you a student, sir?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Students are going first, sir.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: As long as you fill out a slip, you'll be testifying.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And as always, if I mispronounce your name, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just correct it when you speak.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Say your name for the record, okay?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Damaris Amane.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Summer J.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You have a great book recommendation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Anelis Caraballo Cruz.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Madison James.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Olivia Wright.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you have an order in which you've decided you're speaking?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You what?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, I will let you all determine the order in which you speak.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And just say your name for the record, make sure the microphone's on.

chapters.summary: Madison James, a junior at Edward R. Murrow High School, describes her journalism experience reporting on class size and curriculum. She asks DOE to make journalism education accessible to every NYC public high school student through the Portrait implementation plan.
chapters.title: Madison James, student journalist, urges journalism in Portrait implementation

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: State your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: My name is Madison James.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then you may begin your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Again, my name is Madison James, and I'm a junior at Editor Murrow High School in Brooklyn, represented by Councilmember Farrah Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Thank you for hearing our stories today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: As a student journalist for five years and now editor in training at the Murrow Network, I've used journalism to understand my community,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: ask questions that matter, and give people a platform to be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Our journalism program has existed since 1974, and I inherited decades of students and teachers who built a culture where student voices matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Last year, I was able to report on how statewide policies are affecting my school, including the class size mandate and new curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: I spoke with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: teachers and students living with those decisions, researching complicated information, listening to different perspectives, communicating accurately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Investigating those policies also introduced me to an interest in pursuing public policy that I might never have discovered otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: That is critical thinking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: That is effective communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: That is civic engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: And journalism makes students practice those skills for a real purpose, not just for another grade on a transcript.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Journalism also gives students space to critically examine the media they consume, recognize bias, and understand how information shapes public life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: That is why journalism fits so naturally into Port of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: The POG calls for students to become critical thinkers, effective communicators, innovators, global citizens, and future-focused learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Journalists question information and evaluate evidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: We interview people whose experiences differ from our own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: We find creative ways to tell stories, to obtain new information, and communicate them clearly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: We think about how our reporting affects the communities we cover and what we will do better next time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Yet only a quarter of New York City public high schools can provide students with that critical experience, limiting whose voices get the opportunity to be heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: If a Port of a Graduate is preparing students to learn, grow, work, and contribute, journalism gives the place to practice all four.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: I'm asking the DOE to make journalism education accessible for every New York City public high school student through the Port of a Graduate implementation plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: I've had a microphone since sixth grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madison James
utterances.text: Every student deserves the chance to find their voice and know that someone

chapters.summary: Damaris Mañay, a junior at Brooklyn Emerging Leaders Academy, says journalism allowed her to write in Spanish and English and see her culture and language as strengths. She asks for support for bilingual student journalists.
chapters.title: Damaris Mañay describes how bilingual journalism helped her find her voice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: My name is Damaris Mañay, and I'm a student at Brooklyn Emerging Leaders Academy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I also know as Bella.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I'm a junior and a part of my school's journalism program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: At Bella, journalism gives students space to share stories, ask questions, and talk about things that matter to our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: One of the things that has made journalism meaningful to me is being able to write in both Spanish and English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: My parents have always encouraged me to learn English because they know how important it is for my future, school, and everyday life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: As I learned English, I sometimes felt like I had to choose between using English and holding on to Spanish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: Journalism helped me see things differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I realized that I do not have to choose one language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I can use both.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I can write in English and communicate with a wider audience, but I can also write in Spanish and connect with people who share my language and culture.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: Being bilingual is celebrated in journalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: It means a lot to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: My language are part of my identity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: Journalism has helped me become more confident in my own voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I'm not just learning how to write.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: I am learning that my experience, my culture, my language, and my perspective are worth sharing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: For me, journalism is not only about reporting stories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: It is also about making people feel, seen, and heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Damaris Mañay
utterances.text: Being able to use both of my language reminds me that I do not have to leave one part of myself behind to find my voice.

utterances.speaker: Speaker
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm here for any questions that you might have for her.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: No tengo preguntas.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Tus palabras fueron bonitas.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Es claro que este programa es importante por tu...

utterances.text: Estoy emocionado que está aquí a hablar.

utterances.text: Y también la gente del Departamento de Educación está aquí también.

utterances.text: Entonces, ¿sabe cómo importante es este programa?

chapters.summary: Samra Jara, a junior at BELLA, explains how the IB learner profiles align with Portrait attributes. She describes writing an article on ICE that developed her communication, critical thinking, global citizenship, and academic preparedness.
chapters.title: Samra Jara connects International Baccalaureate learner profiles to Portrait and journalism

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: My name is Samra Jara.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: I'm a current junior at BELLA, short for Brooklyn Emerging Leaders Academy, which is the only full IB school and all-girl charter high school located in the Bed-Stuy area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: To understand how our school system meets the requirements of Portrait of a Graduate with journalism, one must first understand the International Back Your Let program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: The International Back Your Let program consists of 10 learner profiles, five of which already align with the six key attributes of POG, Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Those being critical thinkers, knowledgeable, communicator, open-minded, and reflective.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Now you may be wondering, where does journalism play into this?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Journalism is the main component here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Students and learners gain the key attributes of POG through journalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Last year, I wrote an article for my school newsroom, The Hive, that mentioned political stances and the ongoing situation involving ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: When writing this article, I acquired the effective communicator attribute, critical thinker attribute, global citizen attribute, and academically prepared attribute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Four attributes from Portrait of a Graduate through journalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: When pitching this idea to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Lauren, my journalism teacher, I went through various stages of reporting that included analyzing data, researching, and interviewing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Being an effective communicator happened when publishing this article and speaking against the injustices towards my community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Being a global citizen was enabled when interviewing the people who were impacted by ICE and even the people who had their own opinions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: All these students and staff who

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: who have decided to come here and participate are here because they are passionate about including journalism in all schools for education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Samra Jara
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Olivia Wright, a senior at MELS, says she took all Regents and also completed projects. Projects helped her collaborate, retain content, and develop public speaking and time management skills. She supports Portrait while noting Regents can still be useful.
chapters.title: Olivia Wright says project-based learning and Regents together build skills

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Olivia Wright and I'm a senior at Metropolitan Extrusionary Learning School, also known as MELS, and I'm a student advisor for NYC Albert Bound Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: When I think about having this type of conversation, I think about my best friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: She's a special person and has my back no matter what.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: I have friends like her because I go to a special school like Mel's.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: Mel's is a place where to graduate I have to have both took my regents, passed them, and demonstrate my learning through projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: Because of the projects we did, it gave me a way to collaborate with other students and helped me learn through a perspective that wasn't just my teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: It also gave me a way to make friends, not just outside of school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: I know everyone is having mixed feelings about the Regents no longer being a graduation requirement because they're concerned it's going to affect our success in the future and won't be a challenge for us, but I don't think that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: As someone who has taken all of her Regents and does projects to show my learning,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: I can say that the projects have given me skills to be successful in the future and have also helped me pass the regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: For example, taking the history region was easier for me because I have a love for history and the projects I made along the way helped me understand and retain the content I was learning easier.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: In my history class last year, for our final product, we had to get into groups of three to four and put on a performance about a historical figure in the founding era.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: The project was not only fun, but it also gave me and my peers a chance to build team working skills, team building skills, and public speaking skills, and time management skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: Those are skills that I need for work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: I think while assessing everyone the same way, like with regents, is a good thing, schools can begin to take away from what really can help us students be successful, when its main focus is just passing a test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: In my opinion, what can help students be successful is teaching us how to learn, collaborate, and be social.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: Math, science, English, and history are important, but can we really express this knowledge without having these skills?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Olivia Wright
utterances.text: These skills can start to develop through the project-based learning.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can you, if anyone's like a quick 10 seconds, like how does the work done,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
