chapters.summary: Charlotte Arzuian, a junior at Bard Early College Manhattan, introduces a panel of six students and two YJC representatives. She argues journalism develops critical thinking and civic responsibility central to Portrait of a Graduate and asks for journalism in all 500 high schools.
chapters.title: Charlotte Arzuian and Youth Journalism Coalition students present on journalism and Portrait

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sarah Vasquez-Leighton, Kiara Capurso, CJ Sanchez, and Sophie Mode.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Chair Dinowitz, would you be open to our entire student panel coming up?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: How many are there?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: It's six students, then me and Sophie.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: That's one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Pull up another chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is it Ezin Nwanko?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that the panel?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Ezin Nwanko, Charlotte.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Arzuian?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Kamani Mitchell, Julius Marinov.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Please, in your test, state your name for the record and begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Sharla Arzuian.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: I'm Sharla Arzuian, a junior at Bard High School, Early College Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Thank you all for the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: This summer, I interned for the Youth Journalism Coalition, investigating Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Sitting next to me are five New York City public school students and two YJC representatives from across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Today we are going to show you why journalism education is a key to building the skills and scholarly habits central to Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: I go to a school that doesn't teach to the regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: We do take the required number of regents exams, but our learning is focused elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: We take accredited college classes in which we read texts, share our interpretations, and probe those of our classmates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Those conversations are meaningful because they help me develop my voice and my thinking and teach me how to explore open-ended questions where there is not one correct answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: In other words, I resonate with the potential of Portrait of a Graduate because I've benefited from the style of learning in my classes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: When I joined my student newspaper, The Bardvark, I realized student journalism is a natural extension to this learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Like seminars, reporting taught me to approach an issue from multiple angles and sparked a curiosity about the history of my community that got us to where we are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: When the phone policy at my school first came out, I had questions about how the policy would be implemented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: I was able to ask these questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: While reporting and writing on the story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: I also researched state law and interviewed administrators, giving me the tools to clarify the policy for the student body and to approach the issue from multiple angles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Being a journalist not only enabled me to ask these questions, but helped me build communication and critical thinking skills, in this case serving as an important act of civic responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Portrait of a Graduate is a commitment to prepare graduates to think critically and participate in their community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: This is a noble commitment I stand for, and I think involving as many high school students in journalism as possible would be a highly effective way for the city to do this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: With the launch of Journalism for All in 30 schools and a summer internship pipeline built through the Summer Youth Employment Program, the infrastructure already exists to make equitable youth journalism a reality and portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: YJC is ready to work with both the DOE and City Council to help integrate this framework citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Before every interview, I'm so little nervous, but excited at the opportunity to learn more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: I know that now more than ever, we need journalists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Students who have a duty to report on the truth, craft it as a team, and share it with others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: I'm lucky that I'm out of school with a great newspaper, for which I now serve as opinions editor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: But everyone deserves this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Please help give students in all 500 high schools the resources to engage in an important pillar of our democracy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Charlotte Arzuian
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Charlotte.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Apologies, is this working?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Julius Marinov, a senior at High School for Environmental Studies, says his school's journalism club is underfunded and may not survive. He cites Baruch College research that 73% of NYC public high schools lack a journalism program and asks DOE to build journalism into Portrait.
chapters.title: Julius Marinov describes struggling journalism club and stratified access to journalism education

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: My name is Julius Marinov.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: I am a senior at the High School for Environmental Studies in the Upper West Side, District 2.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: When it comes to our student-led journalism club, the Ego Eye, it has always struggled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: The lack of funding and attention has left our program to fend for itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: With these concerns, I'm uncertain if the club will continue after my graduation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: I joined the Youth Journalism Coalition as a student leader to gain more citywide support for journalism education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: My time in the coalition has provided me with multiple insights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: First, the issues of our journalism club are not a strife that we face alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: And it's not a lack of student interest issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: There's a deeper systematic issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Access to journalism education across all schools in New York City is deeply stratified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: In 2022, Baruch College research found that 73% of our city's public high schools lack a journalism program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: We don't know where this number stands today, as the New York City Department of Education has failed to provide reliable statistics, even though they're mandated to report on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: However, there is a way where not only existing journalism education programs can improve, but the potential to expand to the 73% of schools that lack them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: With the release of Portrait of a Graduate Standards, one can't help but notice that journalism already

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: does what the portrait of a graduate demands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Last year, I covered the political situation Burkina Faso in my school's newspaper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: I had to synthesize geography, history, and international relations to write one coherent article.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: This emanates the standards for academic preparedness and global citizenship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Not as concepts on a rubric, but as requirements of the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Journalism education further tests students on their competency in the digital age.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: I spent time discerning fact or fabrication during my research.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: This trained my critical thinking skills more than any standardized test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: With attention to limit AI usage and encourage media literacy in schools, I believe journalism education can serve as a place where both these issues can be addressed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Yet what I see in journalism education that shines as the perfect analog for the portrait of a graduate is upon the completion of a piece.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: When I finished my article, I made events that seemed so far away relevant to my peers, so much so that I recall students mentioning the figures highlighted in the article months after its publishing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: That's the beauty of what a portrait of a graduate is asking for, not a paragraph at the end of an essay, but an introspection on the purpose of my words and how they matter, why they matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: If the Department of Education builds journalism into its plan for the portrait of a graduate, programs like mine won't have to rely solely on student survival tactics to stay afloat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: We will finally have the institutional support to become permanent fixtures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: in our schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: I want the journalism program that I work diligently upon to continue, not to be in a list of clubs made by former students that are now just memories.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: We're trying to practice the skills that the portrait of a graduate demands, but we need your help to keep doing it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: If it hasn't been demonstrated enough today,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: The students of New York City want journalism, and the city wants education to change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: And I suggest a solution for both of those wants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Julius Marinov
utterances.text: Thank you for taking so much time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I don't have intention of cutting students off.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you have a little more to say, it's fine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do keep in mind that we are trying to keep it to two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And the purpose of that is also to ensure that other people have the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to shout out really quickly, you know, you mentioned, you know, the journalism program struggling at your school to get the funding.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to highlight two elements.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And one is, as the Youth Journalism Coalition knows, for the first time this year, we are creating a brand new initiative.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Called Journalism for All, which is receiving an over $280,000 investment from the city council to invest in schools like yours to make sure we have these robust programs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think it also speaks to what I think what we all, if we don't articulate, we know that if it's not measured,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It doesn't always get the investment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And once we, and I love that you're talking about measuring this as part of the portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Because once we start measuring it, teachers and principals have more incentive to actually invest.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: The Department of Education has the incentive to invest in it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Even, may I say, private partners have incentives to invest in these programs.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So it's critical that you're here testifying about the importance of...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Including this in the portrait.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And of course, again, want to highlight the council's contribution to this initiative.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Kamani Mitchell, a student at Brooklyn Institute of Liberal Arts, says her school had only an after-school club and administration would not dedicate a teacher. She says YJC has only a 14% acceptance rate due to demand and asks DOE to prioritize journalism in Portrait.
chapters.title: Kamani Mitchell describes lack of in-school journalism and competitive outside programs

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right, Kamani, you're up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Hello, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: My name is Kamani Mitchell, and I attend the Brooklyn Institute of Liberal Arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: My school didn't have a class for journalism, just a small after-school club run by my wonderful teacher, Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Rohan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: My school was supposed to start a class last year because of student and teacher interest, but our admin chose not to dedicate a teacher to it because they couldn't prioritize it over academic needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Because of the citywide demand for journalism opportunities outside of school, it is very competitive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: YGC did a survey of after-school journal opportunities and found there's only 14% acceptance rate because it's impossible to meet the student demands created by the lack of in-school programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: I feel very lucky that I'm with YJC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: I've developed some exposure and have been connected to programs like the Bell Summer Youth Podcast Academy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Practicing journalism has changed me in ways that I could never see myself changing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Before, I couldn't talk to people outside of my own class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: With journalism, I've gained the confidence to not only talk to people who aren't in my immediate group, but allow me to talk to y'all today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Not only that, I've been more involved in my community, not just my school, but New York City as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: I'm grateful that I've had the opportunity to pursue journalism, but not many kids are offered the same opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Kids in the traditional system learn how to read and write paragraphs, but aren't taught that they can use their skills to make a change, let alone use their voice to speak out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Today, the DOE has the opportunity to change that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: If the DOE includes journalism in a portrait of a graduate framework, it affirms the values of teaching journalism, so principals like mine will finally have a reason to prioritize it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: You can make journalism accessible to all and allow students to platform and resources to make a difference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamani Mitchell
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Sarah Vasquez-Layton, an 11th grader at Urban Assembly School for Media Studies, says she was forced into other classes to meet testing and graduation requirements. She could not take journalism until this semester and asks the Council to acknowledge journalism's role in change.
chapters.title: Sarah Vasquez-Layton says testing requirements blocked her from journalism elective

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Good afternoon, City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: My name is Sarah Vasquez-Layton.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I'm an 11th grader at Urban Assembly School for Media Studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I am here today to talk about my education and access to it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I developed my passion for journalism in seventh grade at a private school when I was put in the elective by accident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I immediately fell in love with it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Now, I'm at a public high school that has a journalism elective, but is treated as an afterthought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: My admin and teachers have even asked me to help promote the elective myself because the school doesn't have the resources to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I picked my school because of its name.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Media studies, but I haven't been able to participate in the journalism program because I was forced into other classes to meet testing and graduation requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Finally, this semester I am in the elective, but I didn't just wait until now to grow in journalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I took matters into my own hands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Like Amani, I had to look outside of my school, so I joined YJC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: With this opportunity came many others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Like this summer, I was able to attend the School of the New York Times and study.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: scientific journalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: So when I finally entered my journalism class on Friday the 11th, it felt wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Not because I didn't want to be in it, but because the class is in its beginning stages and it doesn't have the resources to support me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I realized that it could have started in that classroom over a year ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: But classes like journalism are constantly pushed aside because our current system prioritizes standardized testing over everything else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Regents exams force us to dismiss information that doesn't seem relevant to a test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I have experience having to skip half a textbook just to prepare for an exam six months away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Valuing test scores over actual meaningful learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I am glad the state is taking action through the portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: But I need you to take another thing with you on this journey of changing education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Acknowledge that the change that has happened in our history has been because of journalists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: We need people to speak the truth, ask hard questions, and be our messengers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Journalism teaches us how to do that.

chapters.summary: Ezene Wonkwah, an 11th grader at Medgar Evers College Preparatory School, says her school's journalism program died off. Through YJC she developed communication, critical thinking, and perspective-taking, and asks DOE to make journalism a core part of Portrait.
chapters.title: Ezene Wonkwah describes lost journalism program and skills gained through YJC

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: My name is Ezene Wonkwah and I'm a current 11th grade student at Medgar Evers College Preparatory School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: I have decided to be here on a school day to emphasize the importance of incorporating and expanding journalism programs in more schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: I currently attend a school that doesn't have an active journalism program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: We did have a newspaper and journalism club at a point, which died off over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Through my experience with journalism in YJC as a student leader, I can confidently say that the lack of journalism opportunities puts us at a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Journalism, which started off as a slight interest for me, has become something that has helped me further develop many important skills such as effective communication and understanding of different perspectives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: It's also really important towards critical thinking and writing skills, which are crucial for students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: The exposure to multiple perspectives and knowing what's going on around them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: The reason I have been able to further develop these skills with journalism is because I've sought it outside of my school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Meanwhile, I recognize that not every student has the same access to those experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Oftentimes when I bring up journalism, I am met with it being viewed as a niche interest and some simply not having enough exposure to know what it has to offer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Creating journalism as a core

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: part of students' educational experience as possible through Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Through journalism, students can learn more and display the civic and critical thinking skills learned over the year, making it a perfect fit.

chapters.summary: Kiara Caperso, a junior at Bronx High School of Science, describes her school's strong journalism program. She says students should not have to attend a specialized school or live in a certain zip code to access journalism education.
chapters.title: Kiara Caperso says well-resourced journalism should be available to all students

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Kiara Caperso, and I'm a junior at the Bronx High School of Science.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: When I first became involved in journalism, I thought I was learning to write articles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: I quickly realized I was learning much more than just that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: At Bronx Science, I've had access to a journalism program with the resources to let students do real reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Through my school newspaper, I've interviewed people, reported on issues I care about, learned how to edit, and published stories for an audience far beyond my classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: I've had teachers and editors who pushed me to ask better questions and look more closely at what I was reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: I have been given opportunities to make mistakes, learn from them, and try again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: These opportunities have changed the way I see myself as a journalist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Journalism has taught me to be curious about what I might have missed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: It has taught me how to listen to perspectives different from my own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Most importantly, it has given me the confidence to believe that my questions and my voice are worth pursuing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: But I also recognize that my experience is not universal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: I attend a school where journalism has the resources to support and grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: There are students across New York City who are just as curious.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: motivated, and interested in telling stories, but their schools might lack a journalism class, a publication, an advisor, or the resources to support one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: A student should not have to attend a specialized high school or live in a certain zip code to have the opportunity to discover what journalism can do for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: I know how much students stand to gain from that opportunity because I have experienced it myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: As New York moves towards the portrait of a graduate, we are asking what skills students actually need when they leave high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Journalism answers that question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: It teaches students to think critically, evaluate evidence, communicate effectively, collaborate with others, and engage with the world around them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Those are not skills students learn by memorizing information for a test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: They develop them by asking questions, researching, and reporting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: That is why I believe the question should not be whether journalism education is valuable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Charlotte, Julius, Kamani, Sarah, and Ezine have already proven that it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: The question is whether we are willing to give schools the resources to make that education meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: I've seen what a well-resourced journalism program has given me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: More New York City students deserve that same opportunity, regardless of what school they attend.

chapters.summary: Sophie Mode of the NYC Youth Journalism Coalition describes placing 36 students in paid internships across 11 newsrooms. She says 77% of participants said the program influenced their career aspirations and 90% would recommend it, calling this the true Portrait of a Graduate.
chapters.title: Sophie Mode reports outcomes from Journalism for All summer internships

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: My name is Sophie Mode and I work with the NYC Youth Journalism Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: I'm also a New York City Public School graduate, class of 2021.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: This summer, I had the privilege of overseeing Journalism for All's newsroom internship program, which placed 36 students in paid internships across 11 local newsrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: For six weeks, they were hard at work covering local stories through interviews with community members, written articles, photojournalism, video projects, and creating social media content.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: The program established the first journalism pathway in the Department of Youth and Community Development's Summer Youth Employment Program, connecting classroom learning with the professional news industry and is set to expand for next year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: Every day this summer, I was endlessly inspired by these student journalists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: The questions they asked, the stories they pitched, and the nearly 50 stories they published across their outlets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: They're brilliant journalists and incredible contributors to our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: Above all, I watched them grow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: One student shared that when she started, she was socially closed off and terrified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: By the end, she had made new friends and presented her work in front of a large crowd.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: Her principal even noticed a difference in how she carries herself in the hallways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: During the first week, many students struggled with punctuality, communication, and professionalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: By the final week, those issues had completely vanished.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: From the quality of the emails they sent me to the questions they asked guest speakers, I watched the progression of these students every week.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: The data reflects this impact.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: 77% of participants said the program influenced their career aspirations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: and 90% said they would recommend it to a classmate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: I witnessed firsthand not just the ways in which journalism prepares students to be strong graduates, but for what comes next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: And that is the true portrait of a graduate, that they're ready to start their futures after being New York City public school students, having explored their interests, built technical skills, and with the confidence and readiness to take on college.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: In a professional workplace.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: Isn't this ultimately what we want for every graduate, that they build critical skills and habits and a passion for learning, but above all, the value of being engaged, thoughtful citizens who feel a responsibility to inform their communities about the things that matter to them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sophie Mode
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: CJ Sánchez, director of the NYC Youth Journalism Coalition, thanks the Council for a $280,000 investment in Journalism for All. He says Local Law 27 reports are incomplete and asks DOE to refine reporting methodology and support scalable Portrait implementation through journalism.
chapters.title: CJ Sánchez urges DOE to refine journalism access tracking and support Journalism for All

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Perfect timing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: My name is CJ Sanchez, and I have the honor of serving as the director of the New York City Youth Journalism Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: I want to begin by thanking the City Council on the record for delivering on years of collaboration with our coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: We have moved in lockstep since our first J-Day in 2024 with Council Member Joseph, and with today's historic public investment in the Journalism for All initiative, it is profoundly heartening to see the follow-through and leadership of Chair Dinowitz and other council leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: With the rollout of Portrait of a Graduate, our city has a real opportunity to transform our public education system and confront the segregated access to high-quality schooling that divides our communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: But to actually fulfill this vision, schools need practical methods to meet these new standards without undermining quality, burning out educators, or leaving out students and families trying to navigate a new system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: Journalism for All was built for this, and by supporting this initiative,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: the council is backing a scalable framework for schools to begin implementing Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: As we've discussed, for the DOE to successfully implement and scale these new graduation requirements, they must accurately track school offerings across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: Last year, this council passed Local Law 27 to track journalism access in our high schools, yet the reports released last year and earlier this month are incomplete.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: It omits clubs and publications, it's missing specific course names, and it misidentifies which schools actually offer courses, which we know because we've reached out to every school that was reported to have a course in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: So as we all look out toward the rollout of Portrait of a Graduate, we encourage the DOE to refine their reporting methodology, empowering middle schoolers and their families to make informed decisions about their high school applications, and allowing the city and partners like us to direct resources where they're needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: This work requires dedicated leadership, and we trust Supervising Superintendent Alan Chang's expertise and commitment to meaningful student-centered future-focused learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: We look forward to deeper collaboration with his team, because ultimately, this is about much more than just fulfilling graduation requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: I envision a city where every young person has the tools to think critically, communicate effectively, and actively participate in our democracy, a reality made possible by ensuring high-quality journalism education is accessible and thriving in every public high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - CJ Sánchez
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and for listening to the students today and every day.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks for a quick example of journalism changing a student's perspective. Sarah Vasquez-Layton describes researching Colombia's new president and changing her political view after investigating different sources.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks student journalists about changing their views through reporting

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: A perfect timing also.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I think you saw the time going.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You started speeding up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I was on a bingo sheet.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Kiara, who is your teacher for journalism?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kiara Caperso
utterances.text: Thorpe.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, First Deputy Chancellor, you want to hear something?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Another thing, that guy was my senior high school English teacher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Alexander Thorpe.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just saying, it's funny.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You see, you're learning something new about me every time you're here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And second, maybe just from one or two of you, just really quick, can you just describe in 15 seconds, has there ever been a time where you felt you felt very strongly about an issue?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And then through your work in journalism, through researching it, interviewing people, you kind of...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know, thought differently about the issue afterwards, maybe even changed your position?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sarah, do you want to share a little bit, just, you know, 15 seconds story so everyone can hear about it?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: This year, my native country, Colombia, gained a new president.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: And I had initially stuck with the political party for quite a while until I actually got information from a lot of my family and friends who saw different insight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: So I started investigating and looking at different news and the facts and everything you could see around it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Vasquez-Layton
utterances.text: I changed my point of view, and I stuck with the one who's now president, Abel Lardo Espirella, and he actually has a lot of different point of views as the one that I was following before.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, I think...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: especially given this time in our country, that's what we want all of our, not just students, what all of the residents of this country to do is like critically think about the positions and beliefs that they have,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: second guess themselves, and then do research.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I think, Sarah, you just explained really well that journalism brings that to our country.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I know the first deputy chancellor cares very deeply about civics education.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And your story highlights, I think, how deeply interconnected journalism is to civics education.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz calls Irvin Guato, Melissa Michelle, Angel Tejada, Jose Jimenez, and Eduardo Antonetti to testify. Staff helps seat the panel and confirms speaking order.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls next public testimony panel

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I want to thank this panel for testifying today, and I will call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Irvin Guato, Melissa Michelle, and Angel Tejada.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Jose Jimenez, Eduardo Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Oh, not there where I was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: That's where you were.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: I think we hang on to it for now.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Jose, why don't you sit here?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you want to go last?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll start with you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Would you state your name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In the microphone.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Whenever you're ready.

chapters.summary: Melissa Michelle, a 12th grader from Haiti, describes passing six PBATs including a social studies paper on the Lenape. She says presenting to a panel and internships built her confidence and leadership skills.
chapters.title: Melissa Michelle describes PBATs and internships at International High School at Prospect Heights

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: My name is Melissa Michelle, and I'm from Haiti.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I've lived in the United States for three years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I'm a 12th grade student at International High School at Prospect Heights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I love everything about my school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: At my school, there is no bullying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: We get help when we need it from our advisor and teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Always help us with our work and push us to do more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Also, our counselor helps us apply for jobs and internship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: My school has many clubs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I'm in soccer, softball, French, Asian clubs, dance, and there are more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: To graduate from my high school, we have to pass six P-BATs, native language, English, science, social studies, and personal statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: The people that I enjoyed doing was social studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: As a newcomer to New York, I think it is important to know about its history.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: The focus of my research was on the Lenape Native American people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: people of New York, and why we no longer speak Lenape.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: In my research thesis, I argued that the first removal had the biggest impact on the Lenape people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I wrote this research paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: It was graded by all the teachers, and after I passed the paper, I was allowed to present it to a panel of teachers and students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: It was challenging because they had to ask me questions about what I learned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I had to pass my panel so I could graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Doing PBATs helped me develop my writing, research, and presentation skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Another thing that is special about my school is that we work in group in class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: This helps me prepare for the future because listening to different opinions is very important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: In my class, I have students that speak different language.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: There's always a debate going on, and that's what makes this subject interesting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Working in groups makes you open-minded and more social.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: It teaches you to problem-solve and to be prepared and organized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Another highlight of my school is the partnership they have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: In 9th and 10th grade, I was an apprentice with the BIM Center, and I've learned a lot of things that will help me with my future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: They trusted me to be a group leader and a project and group manager.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Being in a position like this made me love myself more and motivated me to become a businesswoman.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: As a leader, I learned

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: how to behave so that people trust me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I have a voice and share their opinions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Before the experiences offered at my school, it was hard for me to talk in public or in groups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I've always been very shy to new people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Now I feel comfortable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: When I graduate, I plan to go to college.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I'm interested in studying nursing and business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I'm grateful to be at International High School at Prospect Heights because they made me confident to express myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: I think all students in New York City should have the chance to present their work like we do with P-Bats and have opportunities inside and outside school to prepare them for college and life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Merci.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: De rien.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Melissa Michelle
utterances.text: Ask Spanish to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Muy bien.

chapters.summary: Angel Tejada, 18, from the Dominican Republic, describes attending International Community High School, a 10th grade internship, and Columbia's Summer High School Academy for engineers, where he studied electrical engineering, solar energy, and Python.
chapters.title: Angel Tejada describes Columbia engineering program and internship pathway

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: So, first of things, my name is Angel Tejada.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I will present my statement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: So, there are many things in life that can open many more new doors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: And my school is one of these things.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: My name is Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I am 18 years old and I was born and raised in the Dominican Republic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I came to the United States less than two years ago with my family, full of hopes and dreams to be achieved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: Adjusting to this country was challenging, but I was more focused on continuing my education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I was lucky to find the best school in my life, International Community High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: As a school with many immigrant students, I felt understood and supported.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: We have counselors and internship coordinators who help us gain experience and opportunities to plan our next steps after high school and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: After graduation, I plan to study in a four-year college on a STEM major.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: The number one major I want to study is electrical engineering, followed by mechanical engineering and physics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I relate majors to what I desire to be in the future, an aerospace engineer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I feel more confident about my future thanks to the opportunities in ICHS has offered me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: My 10th grade internship

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: helped me improve my communications and public speaking skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: Then, in 11th grade, from the connections I made in my internship, I was accepted into the Summer High School Academy program for engineers shaped at Columbia University, where I studied

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: electrical engineering for five weeks and learn how solar energy and electricity work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: I also learned coding with Python and how to solve health disparities using technologies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: This has increased my interest not only in studying more electrical engineering, but also in ways that knowledge can be used for humanity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: Thanks to the experiences I dreamed of studying electrical engineering in a highly selective Ivy League program, I wish more students had the opportunity I have at International Community High School.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Gracias.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Hablas como...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: ¿Fuiste nacida aquí?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: No, pero es...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: Hablas, parece que hablas, sí, pero...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Pero tu inglés es muy bien.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Es solo hace dos años.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Estaba muy bien.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angel Alexander Tejada-Grujon
utterances.text: Yo estudié mucho dentro de mi país el inglés en un instituto pequeño.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Es claro que hace mucho trabajo aprender inglés.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: También es claro que tiene un buen programa en tu escuela a ayudar y apoyar tu idioma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ezene Wonkwah
utterances.text: Definitivamente.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Erwin Guato, 18, from Ecuador, attends Pan American International High School at Monroe. He describes a social studies portfolio on vaping and says presentations helped him communicate and prepare for college and career.
chapters.title: Erwin Guato describes portfolio presentations and interest in economics

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: My name is Erwin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: I'm 18 years old.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: I'm from Ecuador.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: And I have lived in the United States for two years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: I go to Pan American International High School at Monroe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: What I like most about my school is the way the teacher helps us learn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: They support us and make sure we understand our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: I also like that my school prepares us for our future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: They help us think about college and what we want to do after high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: After I graduate from high school, I want to go to college and study economic or engineering.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: My school gave me the opportunity to take a course at BNCC, where I learned about how to communicate effectively in the world of international business, and that made me interested in learning about economics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: I want to learn more, improve my skills, and have a good career in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: One school experience that has helped me a lot is doing presentations for our portfolios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: These presentations have helped me feel more

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: comfortable speaking in front of other people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: This is important because I will need this skill for college, job interviews, and my future career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: One example is my social studies pivot, which was very interesting because it was about the harmful effects of vaping on young people's life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: It helped me learn more about the risks of vaping and its effect on young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: When we make our portfolios, we choose a topic, do we share, organize our information, and present it to other people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: From this experience, I have learned how to communicate better, organize my ideas, and speak with more confidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: I have also learned how to connect what I am learning in school to real life and our society.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Erwin Guato
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Gracias.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Lo mismo.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Perfecto inglés.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's just so impressive.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm like really taken by it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Eduardo Antonetti, Senior Director at Internationals Network and a former NYC teacher, says Regents forced him to rush curriculum and teach to the test. Internationals' performance-based assessment system allowed rigorous, authentic demonstrations and individualized support.
chapters.title: Eduardo Antonetti contrasts Regents teaching with Internationals performance assessment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: Esteemed Chair Denowitz and members of the Committee on Education, my name is Eduardo Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: I am Senior Director of Advancement and Advocacy for International Network, but today I would like to share my testimony from my perspective as a longtime educator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: I started my career as a proud New York City public school teacher about 30 years ago at Brooklyn International High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: Since then, I've worked in four school districts in New York and Pennsylvania as a teacher, school administrator, and district leader.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: I have the unique perspective of having

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: helped develop and implement international performance-based assessment system, including graduation portfolios, and also having taught global history regions courses and scoring regions exams at a traditional near-state school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: Whereas the Regents forced me to fly through a one-size-fits-all curriculum, teach a decade or more of history per 44-minute class,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: skip time-intensive projects that promote deep learning, and teach to the test, the International's approach instead allowed me to tailor the curriculum and instruction to best meet students'diverse learning needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: International's performance-based assessment system allowed me to challenge students to engage in academically rigorous activities, to demonstrate their learning in meaningful and authentic ways, and to reflect upon and have real ownership of their learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: I mentored small groups of seniors as their graduation portfolio advisor and got to know them well so I could provide individualized support as they work towards academic excellence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: Working with my colleagues at Internationals, we develop rubrics, guidelines, and best practices that are strongly aligned with the Portrait of a Graduate framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: The Portrait of a Graduate should not be reduced to just decoupling from the region's exams or simply hiring a college and career coordinator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: It is an opportunity to transform public education in New York City, and Internationals Network and our affinity partners stand ready to provide support for this initiative because the education and futures of New York City students are at stake.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eduardo Antonetti
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And last on this panel.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Jose Jimenez, a graduate of International High School at LaGuardia and Senior Director at Internationals Network, says his own experience as an immigrant multilingual learner matches Portrait attributes. He urges the Council and NYCPS to recognize Internationals Network as a model and partner.
chapters.title: Jose Jimenez describes Internationals Network as ready partner for Portrait transition

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dinowitz and members of the Committee on Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: My name is Jose Jimenez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: I'm a proud graduate of International High School at LaGuardia Community College and Senior Director of Finance and Operations at the Nonprofit International Network for Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: International's network and affinity partner to NYCPS supports a network of 17 schools in Queens, Brooklyn, the Bronx, and Manhattan, as well as a national network of schools for newly arrived immigrant multilingual learners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: International's network also partners with other schools, districts, educators, and leaders beyond that network to put our proven approach into practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: When I entered international high school as a 12-year-old immigrant learning English, I was not asked to wait until my English was perfect before taking on challenging work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: I learned language and academic content together through hands-on projects, collaboration, presentations, and experiences beyond the classroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: Those experiences taught me to communicate across differences, solve problems, reflect feedback, and take the responsibility for my learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: I wanted to graduate from college and graduate school, the first person in my family to do so, and to devote more than 20 years to public service in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: That is why the New York State portrait of a graduate feels familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: Its six attributes, including academic preparation, critical thinking, effective communication, and global citizenship, describe the Eddie.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: I received and the approach International's Network has helped schools and educators put into place for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: As New York expands the way students demonstrate learning, portfolios, performance-based assessment, project-based learning, work-based learning, and early college experiences can make graduation requirements more meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: Newcomer multilingual learners deserve rigorous opportunities to show what they know and can do so while developing English, not their potential reduced to one test score.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: I urge the Council and New York City Public Schools to recognize International Network, our network schools, and the many schools and educators with support in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: As models and partners in this transition, including students and alumni.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: As well as ex-people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jose Jimenez
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And to all the adults here, you can always submit the rest of your testimony in writing, and it'll be on the record.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank this panel for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Gracias.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Merci.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And next we have Tabitha Peterson, Eric Lee, Rianne Bato, and Seaver Chen.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, you may begin when ready.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: We'll start, unless you have an order you've already prepared, we'll start from my left, your right, and go down.

chapters.summary: Seaver Chen, a senior at Curtis High School and ASAP youth advocate, says being targeted by racist jokes in middle school was brushed off by faculty. He argues schools need restorative justice and culturally responsive adults so students feel safe and can become effective communicators.
chapters.title: Seaver Chen describes race-based bullying and need for restorative justice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: First, I want to thank Chair Dinowitz and the rest of this council for allowing this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: My name is Steve R.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: Chen, and I am a senior at Curtis High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: I'm also a youth advocate with the Asian American Student Advocacy Project, ASAP, which is CACF's youth leadership program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: To me, being academically prepared goes beyond knowing the answers to pop quizzes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: It means to be able to go to school knowing you will be given the tools to learn to your fullest ability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: It also means to go to school knowing you have an environment where you feel safe physically and mentally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: A student's learning environment is important as it shapes social and communication skills as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: But in order to become an effective communicator, students need a space where they are able to express themselves freely without any sense of judgment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: And as of today, this is just not the case in a lot of our schools, therefore making it more challenging to become academically prepared and an effective communicator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: On a personal note, I experienced this feeling in middle school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: As an Asian student in a predominantly white school, I was the target of many discriminatory jokes, met left and right with comments about my eyes and my expected grades in math.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: It felt like a hopeless and lonely situation, and part of the humiliation was due to not having an environment in my school where I could talk about these issues along with my feelings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: This was especially apparent when I brought up being the target of a racist joke to school faculty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: They simply brushed it off, gave me some tissues for my teary eyes, and assured me I would be fine since the student who called me that would be moving anyways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: A few weeks later, he moved away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: And we had a generic assembly slogan, stop bullying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: I wasn't seen, my feelings felt invalidated, and my true needs weren't met.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: What happened to me has been lived by countless students, especially from the Asian American community across generations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: When students feel that they don't have anywhere or anyone to turn to in their learning environment, they continue not to speak up about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: In my situation, I left the office thinking, what good did speaking up do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: And this further causes race-based bullying and harassment to persist in schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: In order to combat this, we need to invest in giving students a space where they know that incidents such as these will be responded to with empathy, communication, and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: Restorative justice programs implemented in schools provide students the space that they're looking for, along with the culturally responsive adult that they can feel free to talk to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: A simple conversation focused on my feelings and the impact those words had on me with the other student would have meant infinitely more to me than a broadly centered assembly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: We need to ensure that more schools continue to embed restorative justice programs into their school culture in order to create a space where students can arrive every day academically prepared and ready to learn to effectively communicate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Seaver Chen
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.
