utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I do want to highlight that in the administration proposed a budget that actually

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Hutt were sort of justice programs, and it was this council that got, there was a sort of justice programs funding restored, along with, you know, the mental health continuum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I appreciate you talking about the bullying and race-based bullying, because it's something that we don't have good reporting on, something we have brought up with the DOE and work that continues to need to be done.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I appreciate you bringing that up.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rian Bato, a senior at Jamaica Gateway to the Sciences and ASAP advocate, says she felt isolated as one of few Filipinos and faced stereotypes. She calls for inclusive curriculum, mental health support, and global citizenship education.
chapters.title: Rian Bato describes isolation as Filipino immigrant and need for inclusive curriculum

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: First, I want to thank Chair Dean Witz and the rest of the council for allowing this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: My name is Rian Bato, and I am a senior at Jamaica Gateway to the Sciences High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: I'm also a youth advocate with the Asian American Student Advocacy Project, ASAP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: In my perspective, being a global citizen is being open to people who come from different backgrounds and understanding that everyone has their own unique experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: This means actually taking time to listen and learn from others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: I was born in the Philippines and only recently moved to New York in 2022.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: As one of the few Filipinos in my school, I felt isolated.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: I had nobody else who related to my experiences, and it felt like I didn't have a community in school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: My peers made assumptions about me based on my AAPI identity and expected me to fit certain stereotypes, like being smart and quiet.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: If my school had prepared us all to be global citizens with an inclusive curriculum that helps students learn, understand different backgrounds and experiences, along with support to help students like me navigate cultural changes, I would have been...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: better prepared to thrive academically and socially.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Being a global citizen requires us to be reflective and future focused as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: To me, this means being able to look back on my own experiences, recognize how they shaped me, and think about how I can use what I learned to make things better in the future for others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: When I was stressed or struggling, it could feel like I was supposed to handle it all by myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: These experiences made me realize how difficult it can be to take care of your mental health when you don't always feel comfortable speaking up or showing that you're struggling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: I know many other AAPI youth like myself have felt the same way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Many AAPI students deal with stereotypes, academic pressure, cultural expectations, and stigma around mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: The model minority myth pushes this even further by making AAPI students feel like they have to struggle on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Schools have a responsibility to help students become global citizens, reflective, and future-focused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: But they often put so much focus on grades that students don't get opportunities to learn about different cultures, the time to have meaningful conversations, or to reflect on their own experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: If schools can create spaces and opportunities for this, students can become more understanding of others while also learning how to take care of themselves and their communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rian Bato
utterances.text: Salamat po.

chapters.summary: Eric Lee, a senior at Queens High School for the Sciences and ASAP advocate, says he translates for his parents and peers fear speaking due to broken English. He calls for real language access, culturally responsive curriculum including AAPI history, and measuring belonging.
chapters.title: Eric Lee describes language access barriers for multilingual students and families

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: To begin, I'd like to acknowledge and thank Chair Dinowitz and members of the City Council for allowing this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: My name is Eric Lee, and I'm currently a senior at Queens High School for the Sciences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: I'm also a youth advocate with the Asian American Student Advocacy Project, ASAP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: I believe that academic preparedness plays a crucial role in helping multilingual students like me thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: As a student, being academically prepared does not simply mean having access to the information needed to succeed academically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Rather, it means having access to the resources necessary to learn without fear or self-doubt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Multilingual students require much more than just translation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: They require instruction that acknowledges their identity and supports them through teacher training that specifically addresses multilingualism and diversity of language background.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Secondly, for me, an effective communicator is someone who has a supportive environment to communicate their thoughts and ideas regardless of culture or language barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Students should be able to express themselves freely without concern about the judgment of others based on their language skills.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Schools should provide an environment where all students'voices are valued, where language differences or barriers do not limit the voice of a student.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: As a student from the AAPI community, I frequently translate school documents for my parents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: In addition, due to the lack of systems supporting immigrant families at school, I had to act as a translator between my family and teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: I've also observed some of my peers refrain from speaking up during classroom conversations because they fear how their broken English will be judged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: These examples provided are not unique to my own story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: When students are denied adequate language access, they are unable to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: to fully participate in class discussions, restorative justice circles, or collaborative learning activities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: While the DOE assesses test scores and graduation rates as indicators of student success, they do not assess whether students feel linguistically supported or if they believe they have the ability to speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: With pressure placed upon teachers to prepare students for standardized testing, opportunities for educators to engage students through restorative practices or multilingual engagement continue to decrease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: We need to invest in real language access from translated materials to inclusive school environments so every student can participate fully as an effective communicator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: We need to embed a culturally responsive curriculum, including AAPI history, so students feel represented, supported, and academically prepared.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Finally, we need to measure belonging, not just test scores, so schools are held accountable for creating environments where all students can learn, speak, and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I do want to highlight two important things.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: One is you have a Queens High School for Science.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You have a great graduate right here.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Our committee counsel, Alejandro Carvajal, also went there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: He just graduated two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So he's, you know, the same age as you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And also, you know, I think it's so important for all the different communities around our city to be seen and heard.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And that's why this council has invested, I think at this point, millions of dollars over the years in the AAPI curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So, you know, we're doing this work in this council, but of course it means nothing without students like you coming to testify and sharing your voice.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And last in this panel.

chapters.summary: Tabitha Peterson, a junior at Brooklyn Technical High School and ASAP advocate, says critical thinking and cultural awareness are key to safe spaces. She says lack of AAPI history and the model minority myth harm minority students and calls for inclusive curriculum and bridge building.
chapters.title: Tabitha Peterson says inclusive curriculum and cultural awareness create safe classrooms

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: First, I want to thank Chair Dinowitz and the rest of the council for allowing this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: My name is Tavi, and I'm a junior at Brooklyn Technical High School.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: I'm also a youth advocate for the Asian American Student Advocacy Project, ASAP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: What does it take to create a truly safe space?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Well, a whole bunch of factors, really, with two of the most important ones being critical thinking and cultural awareness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: I understand critical thinking to be the ability to take in your surroundings with observations and create thoughtful inferences based on what you observe, and define cultural awareness as being thoroughly educated on your own social identity and how it can impact your interactions slash relationships with others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: When I walk into the classroom, the first thing I want to be is open-minded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Not only does this make classroom conversations more conducive, but it also lets the people around me know that their presence is welcome.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Being aware of my cultural background, like my race and ethnicity, and how it can indicate ways in which I'm similar and different from my peers, grants me the ability to be sure that I'm creating an inviting space for everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Unfortunately, a common problem that minorities face in the classroom is a lack of knowledge about their own history and impact in America.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: In the case of the AAPI community, there is a severe lack of inclusive curriculum.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: This in turn makes it difficult to foster a thoughtful environment and perpetuates an uncomfortability for the AAPI community and other minorities while in the classroom and even in their everyday lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: I can say that I have witnessed firsthand the result of shared unawareness creating

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: misunderstanding and discomfort in my own community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Often in the black student union of my school, there is talk about demographics of the student body and how it makes us feel uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: One time there was a conversation that mentioned how the majority of students in the school are AAPI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Because of what I've learned in spaces like ASAP, I could see how the model minority myth harmfully impacted and shaped the conversation that unfolded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Now, if our school had included AAPI history into the curriculum, students would be educated on the model minority myth and learn that it is completely untrue and should be dismantled while minorities focus on bridge building and solidarity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: Although our struggles are different, minorities should be able to find community with each other instead of fighting to be second place in a hierarchy that shouldn't even exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Peterson
utterances.text: This is just one example of how inclusive curriculum and shared understanding across differences can help support critical thinking, cultural awareness, and ultimately school safety for all students.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz thanks student leaders and calls Ariana Misha, Jeannie Ferrari, Xavier Otero, Bashir Joara, Vera Shengalia, and Eric Levine to testify.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls next panel including educators and advocates

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Seeing student leaders come up here and testify is really inspiring.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you for coming up today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to call the next panel, Ariana Misha.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Jeannie Ferrari.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Xavier Otero.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Bashir Joara.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Vera Shengalia.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Eric Levine.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh, and whole folders.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh.

chapters.summary: Jeanne Ferrari, principal of Humanities Preparatory Academy and Beacon School, says consortium schools use performance-based assessments where students research, write, and orally defend college-level work before panels. She asks to sustain the consortium district structure.
chapters.title: Principal Jeanne Ferrari describes consortium performance-based assessments

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dinowitz and members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: My name is Jeanne Ferrari.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Since 2012, I've had the privilege of leading two New York City public schools, both Humanities Preparatory Academy and the Beacon School as principal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Both belong to the New York Performance Standards Consortium, a 30-year network of 38 schools with a state waiver to replace high-stakes regents'examinations with performance-based assessments, or PBAs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Instead of asking students to cram for a one-size-fits-all test, we prepare them to research, write, and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: orally defend what is essentially a college dissertation across four core subjects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Students must present their findings to a panel of educators and outside evaluators who ask rigorous, unpredictable, on-demand questions on the spot in a way that simply cannot be faked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: The process demands critical and creative thinking,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: clarity, and the capacity to communicate your ideas effectively to an outside audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Every single college graduate who has returned to visit me over the years says the PBAT process is the single most important factor that's prepared them for their college education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: None of this would be possible without our innovative district structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Which allows our 38 schools to collaborate across boroughs, unify and align our grading rubrics, and provide the professional development that teachers need to uphold this model over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: To sustain our work and make it a true blueprint for how the city's transition to portrait of a graduate could work,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Our schools must continue to collaborate within our unique consortium internationals and outward bounds district and continue to partner with the New York Performance Standards Consortium

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: who provide the professional development that upholds this model and ensures its high quality across our schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: I am grateful to the New York City Department of Education and the City Council for your time and your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeanne Ferrari
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Xavier Otero, a senior at Middle College High School, says traditional middle school made him shy and test-driven. At consortium school he wrote a social studies PBAT on Elon Musk and government power, became more collaborative, and plans to become a firefighter.
chapters.title: Xavier Otero says Middle College PBATs made him collaborative and future-focused

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Hello, Chair Dinowitz and members of council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: My name is Xavier Otero, and I'm a senior at Middle College High School, which is located on the LaGuardia Community College campus in Long Island City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Middle College is a school of the consortium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Middle College's system of performance assessment is helping me with all the portfolio

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: portrait of graduate component, but I want to focus on how it made me an effective communicator and reflective and future focused.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I came to middle college from a very traditional middle school where the classes were test driven and focused on passing the regents exams in eighth grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Because I was good at math and computer science, and because of all my classes were focused on individual work, I assumed my future job would be sitting alone in a room, working for a company.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I was very shy and nervous to talk to others, especially grown-ups.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: My outlook completely changed at Meadow College, where my ideas and personal...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Individual personality was taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Teachers focused on pushing students'individual passions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I was also allowed to make choices about what I wanted to study and focus on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I wrote my social studies PBAT on how entrepreneurs like Elon Musk should not be given power in government, such as Doge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: In our classes, we are expected to work with our peers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Teachers frequently refuse to answer questions, telling us to talk to each other to struggle out our confusions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: It had pushed me out of my comfort zone, but made me a more collaborative thinker and made me more

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: confident and advocating for myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: This new independence and freedom made me feel excited for what I learned because I chose what I learned.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I've also built skills of planning long-term projects like PBATS, organizing the paper, managing deadlines, and so on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: The freedom also allowed me to plan for the future and take classes that would help me most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I am enrolled in several college classes and plan to get my associate's degree.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I no longer see myself alone in a room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I now work in the community helping others.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: I plan to become a firefighter and perhaps get a degree in psychology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: And I'll be happy to answer any questions you might have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Xavier Otero
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you, Xavier.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Next speaker.

chapters.summary: Ariana Misha, a junior at New York Institute for Collaborative Education, says she left a traditional high school that emphasized AP classes. At NICE she did mock UN, Model UN, debate, and newspaper, and says education should create graduates who can change the world.
chapters.title: Ariana Misha says consortium school let her pursue civics and global activism

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: Hello members of the council and everyone present in this room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: My name is Ariana Misha.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I'm a junior at the New York Institute for Collaborative Education in Manhattan, a member school in the consortium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I began ninth grade in a traditional high school, which emphasized AP classes, leaving little time for extracurricular activities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: That had always been important to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I even quit debating, which I had done for five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: Everyone was just trying to pass tests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I started going to NICE at 10th grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I'm surely learning a lot more than before, because NICE creates pathways for a student to chase their passion, both in and out of school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: My human rights teachers organized a mock United Nations conference in the class rather than just teaching in a traditional way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: And this inspired me to follow my passion for civics and take up Model UN as my extracurricular activity and also serving as a youth delegate at the General Assembly at the United Nations headquarter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I'm currently on the debate team and the president of our newspaper club, and I consider myself a true global citizen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: NICE has allowed me to take my interests in an academy direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: For my neuroscience panel this year, I'll be looking at how the involvement in political activities at an early age has a long-term effect on the brain and personality development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: We as students aren't bound to learn only one thing, determined by someone else, but rather, we get the chance to choose our own passion by making every word reflected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: All consortium schools, including NICE, has banned the use of AI during the pre-bat process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: Our works are project-based, and which doesn't always make us needy to use AI.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: Last year,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: I've done multiple advocacy efforts, which includes fighting against AI with Nightclue and being part of a national and international sustainable development goal campaign.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: My school for me is a place where I grow and learn by interacting with my teachers, calling them by their first name, and gaining confidence and collaborating with my peers for every project, while also being highly active in different social and international activism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: The goal of education should be to create students who knows how to pass a test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: It should not be to create students who knows how to pass a test, but graduates who can actually change the world.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Ariana Misha
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Next speaker.

chapters.summary: Bashir Juara, from Gambia, attended madrasa before moving to the US. At International Community High School he learned English through Greek mythology and completed a PBAT on Zeno's paradox, later graduating from Cambridge with a master's, crediting the consortium model.
chapters.title: Bashir Juara describes path from Gambia to Cambridge via Internationals PBATs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: My name is Bashir Juara.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I come from a country where education access is limited and where students attend different types of schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Growing up in the Gambia, I attended Madrasa, an Arabic school where the curriculum focused primarily on religious studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I had little exposure to English, science, history, or mathematics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I moved to the United States in the summer of 2017.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I had one goal at the time, to enroll in American high school and learn English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I vividly remember going with my uncle to Fordham Plaza to register for school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I wanted to attend traditional American high school because one of my friends attended one at the time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: During the registration, the person assisting me trying to have basic conversation with me in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Although I understand some of what she was saying, I could not respond.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: She paused for a minute and recommended International Community High School in the South Bronx, ICHS, explaining to my uncle that, given my level of English at the time, she did not believe I would thrive in traditional American high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: The recommendation changed my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I arrived at ICHS largely unprepared for academic expectations of an American high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: At the time, I was only confident writing my full name in English, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I still remember being introduced to algebra in 10th grade and seeing equations with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: X's and Y's instead of just numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I remember thinking, this can't be math.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I had barely learned addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division in Arabic, and suddenly I was being asked to solve algebraic equations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: It was intimidating at the time, but ICHS did not treat what I like as limitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Instead, my teachers saw potential and gave me support and encouragement to develop as a thinker and learner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Cora, my first English teacher, introduced me to reading and writing through Greek mythology.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I was fascinated by the stories because they were different to what I have encountered in Marabic studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: At the time, I was struggling to read and write.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Cora was patient with me, encouraging me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: First time was writing full sentences and paragraphs in English.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: She recognized my curiosity and pushed me to express my ideas even when I was struggling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: And similarly, my mathematics experience was equally transparent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: With Ms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Kwame's encouragement, I began writing on performance-based assignment tasks known as PBAT, exploring Zeno's paradox and relationship between finite and infinite.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: At first, I struggled to understand the problem, but the project gave me something I had rarely experienced in school before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: Permission to be curious, ask questions, experiment, and find my path towards an answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: To become observing the project that I would work on equations in the train between work and school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I explored decimals, developed equations, and eventually wrote more than 20 pages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I presented my research before a panel, explained how I developed

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: developed my equation, defended my research findings, and connected abstract mathematic problem to broader equations about real life, including Nelson Mandela's struggle to freedom for justice in South Africa.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you could just summarize your last point.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I know it's a long one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: But to summarize, the consortium school experience has given me an opportunity and made me the learner I think I am today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I just recently graduated from University of Cambridge with my master's in philosophy in development studies, international development studies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: And without the consortium experience at International Community High School, I don't think I would be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: And I think my path would have been completely different.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bashir Juara
utterances.text: I am really grateful for the experience.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Vera Shengalia, parent of a consortium graduate and current Beacon student, says her daughter arrived from a third-world country and found her voice through performance-based assessments. Her daughter now studies at Cooper Union and was prepared to think, not just draw.
chapters.title: Vera Shengalia says performance-based assessment helped her daughter after immigration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Vera Shingelia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: I'm a mom of graduate of Urban Academy and a mom of a student who's in Beacon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: So I know immigrants aren't the most popular group in America right now, but in New York, families like mine aren't the exception.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: We are the huge part of this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: We fled in a third-oriented country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: When we arrived, my daughter, Vasilisa, was one of the many kids starting school here after their whole world had fallen apart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: For a child that feels like landing on Mars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: And I think the most important thing a school can do for that child is show her that not everything is gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Adults still listen and questions are still welcome and her voice still belongs to her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: A child in that state probably won't show her best thinking on a time test on one stressful morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: But give her time, a hard question, and a teacher who pays attention, and you'll see what she can really do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: You cannot teach values through A, B, C, or D.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: They grow through practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: We're writing an essay for the fifth time, defending an idea out loud, fighting for your argument.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: That's what performance-based assessments ask of students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: It isn't the easy option, and no one does it alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: It takes teachers, classmates, a community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Today, Vasilisa studies at Cooper Union.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Entrance days gave her a few abstract prompts and four weeks to turn them into six original concepts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Drawing well wasn't enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: They wanted to see whether she could think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Her consortium school had prepared her for exactly that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: You know that we parents are anxious people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: We are always chasing the next goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: High school, college, good job, good salary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: We rarely stop to ask why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Immigration made me stop.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: When you are running into the unknown with two kids and two suitcases, you remember very fast what matters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: We want our children to be free, honest, and brave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: As someone who fled an authoritarian country, I can tell you that people do not become free, honest, and courageous by learning to choose the correct box.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I do want to address something.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I know that comment, the immigrants aren't the most popular group right now, is probably like a funny little side comment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But I just want everyone watching to know that my office, the council, the Department of Education,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: we do an incredible amount of work to celebrate and uplift our immigrant community because they are so loved.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It may not feel like that in the White House, but it's certainly that way here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I want everyone listening to know that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vera Shengalia
utterances.text: Thank you so much from my family for that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

chapters.summary: Eric Levine, ninth grade social studies teacher and UFT chapter leader at Harvest Collegiate, says he hated his high-performing Regents high school. He now teaches in a consortium school where he can design rigorous, responsive classes that prioritize critical thinking and communication.
chapters.title: Teacher Eric Levine contrasts Regents school with consortium school

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: My name is Eric Levine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I teach ninth grade social studies and lead the UFT chapter at Harvest Collegiate High School, a consortium school near Union Square.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I became a teacher partly because I hated school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: My parents put a great deal of value on education and moved me and my siblings just north of the city to Rockland County due to the reputation of the schools there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: The high school I attended still hovers around the top 50 high schools in the state, and it was a miserable experience for me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: At no point in those four years did I feel like my individuality was honored, that my interests were encouraged, or that I was learning what I would need for after graduation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: As a teen, I became very interested in politics and current events.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I wanted to get involved in the world around me, but my high school never offered an outlet for me to explore that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Instead, much of my time in high school was spent preparing for the New York State Regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I often wondered if there wasn't a better way to educate students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: So imagine my excitement when just weeks into my training as a teacher, I found that there were more than a dozen schools working together to do something better than the regions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Once I learned of the New York State Performance Standards Consortium, I never wanted to be or teach anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: In the past 11 years, I've visited many of those schools and in every single instance have thought to myself, I wish I went to high school here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I taught in a traditional region school for a few years, waiting for the opportunity to work at a consortium school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: My time was filled with prepackaged curriculum, rushed lessons in units, and a lack of rigorous work and deep thinking for my students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I did what I could, but at the end of the day, they needed to pass these tests.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: My school bragged about its high graduation and college acceptance rates, but never reflected on or commented on its low college retention rates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: That model simply did not prepare students for the rigors and demands of what comes after high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Consortium schools like mine

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Better prepare students for what they will encounter after they leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: I have the freedom to design classes that are responsive to their interests and lives, that are deep and rigorous, and that are rooted in skills that will set them up for success after they graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: There is no mad dash to cover 300 years of human history in nine months.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Classes become living, breathing things that force students to think deeply about the world around them and make connections to their own lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: These classes prioritize critical thinking, reflection, and effective communication, as do the project-based assessments they lead to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: They prepare students to be the global citizens that we hope they will be for the rest of their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Eric Levine
utterances.text: Working in a consortium school allows me and my colleagues to provide the kind of educational experience to hundreds of students that I wish I had been able to have had myself.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right, fellow chapter leader, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You can begin whenever.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't know if you have any.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh, they're all done.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank this panel for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Really appreciate it and appreciate your stories.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz calls Randy Levine, Daniela Souza-Egarov, Cherie Gibson, Ann Nelson, Jordan Pineda, David Bloomfield, and Kimberly Olson to testify.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls next panel of advocates and researchers

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Next panel we call Randy Levine, Daniela Souza-Egarov, Cherie Gibson, Ann Nelson, Jordan Pineda,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: David Bloomfield, and Kimberly Olson.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Unless you have a pre-planned order, we'll go from left to right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: My left to my right, starting with David.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And just remember to say your name for the record.

chapters.summary: David Bloomfield, Professor Emeritus at Brooklyn College and CUNY Graduate Center, says the state Regents meeting gave no confidence in defining Portrait. He warns exams may persist and return to teaching to the test, and urges the Council to recommend a pause until the field fills in blanks, especially for multilingual learners and students with disabilities.
chapters.title: David Bloomfield urges pause in state regulations until Portrait is defined

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Yes, hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: My name is David Bloomfield, Professor Emeritus, Brooklyn College, and the CUNY Graduate Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Dinowitz, members of the Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Simply put, nothing in last week's Regents meeting gives confidence that the state is ready to define the portrait of a graduate's blurry outlines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Surprisingly, staff even stepped back from their signature renunciation of Regents exams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Despite Deputy Commissioner's memorandum that the exams are inappropriate as graduation requirements or even for grading, they now insist that the exams persist to align curriculum to learning standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Such a proposal would return districts to teaching to the test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: The very problem portrait of a graduate was meant to reform.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: My urgent request is that the council recommend a

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: pause in the region's promulgation of regulations tied to Portrait of a Graduate until the field can fill in the blanks left unrealized by state ed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Call it a clinical trial of Portrait of a Graduate's aspirations before regulations set its structures in stone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Of particular importance are attention to the needs of multilingual learners, students with disabilities, other groups, and local circumstances which state ed has largely ignored in its overall plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: New York City is well positioned to act without state ed's imposing mandates, clearly not ready for prime time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: Deputy Chancellor for High Schools Alan Chang has strong experience as a former superintendent for consortium, international, and expeditionary learning schools,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: the very basis for Portrait of a Graduate's emphasis on project-based experiential curricula and well along in planning without premature state mandates complicating their work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: By putting graduation standards in the hands of educators, not standardized test vendors or politicians bent on inflating class rates, we can bring sanity to end an era when gimmicks like credit recovery

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Bloomfield
utterances.text: substitute for teacher judgment.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Annie Nelson, policy analyst at Children's Aid, says Portrait's success depends on supports and experiences. She highlights community school strategies and urges the Council to establish 100 new community schools by fiscal 2029, prioritizing under-resourced neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Annie Nelson calls for community schools to support Portrait competencies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: Thank you to Chair Dinowitz, the Education Committee, and the New York City Council for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: My name is Annie Nelson, and I'm a policy analyst at Children's Aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: For over 170 years, Children's Aid has worked to ensure that young people face no limits to their aspirations or potential.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: Today, we serve nearly 50,000 children, youth, and families across more than 40 sites citywide, including 19 community schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: As an organization that works in schools and with young people across some of the city's most under-resourced neighborhoods, we know that our education system is not yet preparing every young person for post-secondary success.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: We support the intention behind the Portrait of a Graduate to reimagine the skills that young people need to succeed in college, career, and civic life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: At the same time, changes to graduation requirements should not diminish schools'responsibility to ensure that every student has access to a rigorous and high-quality education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: Its success will depend on ensuring that all students have the experiences and supports needed to develop the portrait's core competencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: The community school strategy can help make this possible by expanding relationships, enrichment opportunities, and academic supports that remove barriers to academic opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: The Essentials for Community School Transformation, developed by four partners, including the National Center for Community Schools at Children's Aid, provides a framework for creating these school-based conditions through practices including expanded learning, community-connected instruction, integrated support teams,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: systems and student and family engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: We see these practices in action across children's aides community schools citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: At Central Park East 2 in Harlem, project-based learning and after-school program connects academics to real-world challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: At Fannie Lou Hamer Freedom High School in the Bronx, college tours and career exploration help students connect their learning to their futures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: And in two of our schools in Washington Heights, through student governments and training in participatory action research, students can use critical thinking skills to identify issues in their school communities and use their findings to drive change as emerging global citizens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: Based on these experiences, we urge the Council on New York City Public Schools to first establish 100 new community schools by fiscal 29, prioritizing schools where students face the greatest act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: Barriers to academic opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I told you, I'm a little tougher on adults than kids.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So, all right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I what?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Annie Nelson
utterances.text: I said we look like him.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh, you...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Daniela Souza Egorov, a parent and Manhattan Institute fellow, says Regents exams have long signaled rigor and accountability. She argues eliminating them will lower diploma value and mask failure to teach basic skills, and calls for school choice.
chapters.title: Daniela Souza Egorov criticizes elimination of Regents exams as lowering accountability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: My name is Daniela Souza-Igorov, and I'm a New York City public school parent and a fellow at the Manhattan Institute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Since the 1800s, the New York Regents exam has indicated academic excellence and rigor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Generations of New York students have studied hard to accomplish this milestone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: It is deeply concerning that the New York Board of Regents will eliminate those exams, and board member Felicia Thomas-Williams said that, quote, you don't assess a fish on climbing a tree because fish can't climb trees.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Quote, why do the people responsible for setting education policy in our state have no confidence in our kids'ability to learn?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: This is just the last act of the Board of Regents to eliminate any accountability in our state after lowering the standards of the state test a few years ago to hide the drop in performance after the extensive closures of schools during the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: New York State now spends nearly $40 billion per year on education, which makes it the most expensive public school system in the country for 19 consecutive years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Unless the portrait of a graduate sets rigorous and objective measures like the regions, it will

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: be another ill-advised decision, which will only try to mask the reality that the majority of our students are not learning basic skills in math and reading at the end of high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: It will lower the value of New York State high school diploma, and it won't solve the actual problem that the New York Board of Regents and this body should be focused on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Making sure our kids, making sure our public schools actually teach our kids or offer school choice for those who are not lucky enough to get a seat in a public charter school or cannot afford to pay for private school or homeschool their kids.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Daniela Souza Egorov
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Oh, 13 seconds to spare.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Sheree Gibson, a NYC public school alum, parent, and Blue Ribbon Commission member, says Portrait came from stakeholder feedback that a Regents-focused system failed to prepare students for post-secondary success. She argues rigor is not found in a one-day exam.
chapters.title: Sheree Gibson defends Portrait as response to students, families, and employers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: You see.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the New York City Council Committee of Education.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: Chair Denevitz, thank you for the opportunity to speak today on the New York State Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: My name is Cherie Gibson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: I'm a proud New York City public school alum, a high school parent, a citywide Title I parent leader, an education advocate who served as a member of the New York State Blue Ribbon Commission on Graduation Measures.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: The portrait of the graduate came out of the recommendations of the commission and is foundational to the systemic change of what education in New York State could be, encompassed in the entire New York Inspires transformative plan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: The portrait of a graduate was a direct answer to what we heard resoundingly from students, families,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: higher education official employers that we have not been preparing our young people for post-secondary success or future past the 21st century.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: A focus on regents, a one-day exam, piecemeal work on providing variety in their students'learning experiences, which was mainly in extracurricular clubs and activities, as you heard from the journalism students today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: Assessing educators'effectiveness just on a standardized exam.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: The, excuse me, rigor has been mentioned a lot today, but it's not found in just a one-day exam.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: The dependence or focus on the regents has minimized the importance of classroom work and participation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: And in looking at additional experiences,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: that we think that there's no other way to assess our students'mastery of a subject is only from a regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: Have you spoken to a teenager lately who's taken a regents?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: They walk out of the regents either saying, whew, man, that was so easy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: We learned that at the beginning of the school year, or nothing we learned this whole school year was on this test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sheree Gibson
utterances.text: And so if we're stating that their rigor, their mastery is to be learned by the exam.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Randi Levine, Policy Director at Advocates for Children, supports multiple pathways and decoupling Regents. She calls for extensive stakeholder engagement, drawing on existing performance-assessment expertise, a comprehensive communications plan, and targeted supports for students with disabilities and multilingual learners.
chapters.title: Randi Levine supports decoupling but urges stakeholder engagement and attention to SWD/ML

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Dinowitz, for holding this hearing and for the opportunity to speak with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: My name is Randi Levine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: I'm Policy Director of Advocates for Children of New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: In addition to helping families navigate New York City schools, including high school graduation requirements, AFC also served on the state's Blue Ribbon Commission on Graduation Measures and coordinates the statewide Coalition for Multiple Pathways to a Diploma.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: We are pleased to see the New York State Education Department move forward with its proposal to decouple Regents exams from graduation requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: AFC has long advocated for multiple pathways to a high school diploma, for a system that provides students with multiple ways to demonstrate what they know and are able to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: And this is especially true given that there is no evidence that exit exams increase student achievement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: And I think you heard from the students here more powerfully than I can ever say the value of those multiple ways and how they have impacted students learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: As this work moves forward to ensure we capitalize on this opportunity, there are many steps that need to be taken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: With our limited time today, we'll highlight just a few recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: First, New York City Public Schools needs to engage in extensive stakeholder engagement with meaningful opportunities for feedback.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools should also draw on the expertise of schools and educators across New York City that are already using performance-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: NYCPS should also start developing a comprehensive community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: communications plan now to ensure students and families understand what they need to do to graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: There are still big questions to answer and it's hard to overstate how critical it will be to get clear and accessible information out to the field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: There must also be an intentional and targeted focus on the needs of students with disabilities and L's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Too often in our work, we see barriers to access and meaningful participation, such as limited supports and accommodations for students with disabilities in certain works-based learning programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: We want to ensure that students with disabilities and L's can get the academic and transition support they need to graduate and to have full access to graduation pathways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Randi Levine
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Jordan Panetta, policy lead at EdTrust New York, says the state's rollout raises concerns about access, comparability, rigor, and accountability. He urges NYSED and the Council to delay implementation and recommends a task force, vetted assessments, competency-based evaluations, and using consortium schools as models.
chapters.title: Jordan Panetta urges delay in New York Inspires rollout over concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: My name is Jordan Panetta, the policy lead on this issue at EdTrust New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: We look forward to sharing our comprehensive written testimony in the coming days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: EdTrust New York has serious concerns regarding the state's rollout, not necessarily the idea of New York Inspires and the portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Specifically, we're concerned that this initiative of being rolled out will create major challenges to New York City public schools that will exacerbate issues of access with the creation of alternative learning pathways, creating challenges in comparing and assessing post-secondary readiness,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: sacrifice rigor by creating learning pathways that are difficult to design and assess between schools and across districts, eliminate any measure of student readiness and system accountability that the region's exams had historically provided,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: and divert investments from essential initiatives like NYC Reads and NY Resolves, which play critical roles in ensuring students are entering high school at the grade level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: EdTrust New York is urging NYSED to delay the rollout of Inspires, including the decoupling of the Regents exams for this next cohort until they address these concerns and provide districts with more holistic implementation guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: We urge the council members to also call for a delay in this implementation and seek clarity with state leadership and the Board of Regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: If Inspires is not delayed, we recommend the city prioritize the following principles as it develops a plan to align with the portrait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: First, we want to convene a task force to design and vet alternative learning pathways and their post-graduation application with key stakeholders, including families and students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Second, provide students with vetted assessment options to demonstrate proficiency in addition to the regions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Third, develop competence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: NC-based evaluations that ensure comparability across districts and schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Fourth, prioritize rigor when designing instruction pathways and rubrics and company-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: And last, look at the 37 consortium schools and their PBATs as scalable models of rigorous and effective 21st century learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Would like to emphasize this last principle.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Finally, I trust believes this is an opportunity for the city to lead as an example for the rest of the state if NYCPS leadership prioritizes collaboration and remains committed to building a readiness system that is rigorous, equitable, and promotes transparency and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jordan Panetta
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Under the wire.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Kimberly Olson, Executive Director of NYC Arts and Education Roundtable, says arts education develops skills aligned with Portrait attributes but Regents exams squeezed arts out. She asks for clear guidance, more certified arts teachers, professional development, and strategic partnerships.
chapters.title: Kimberly Olson says arts education is untapped resource for Portrait

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Dinowitz, Councilmember Wong, the Education Committee and City Council staff for hosting today's oversight hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: My name is Kimberly Olson, and I'm proud to be the Executive Director of the New York City Arts and Education Roundtable, also proud graduate of New York State Schools, having taken many Regents exams in my time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: As our city maps out this next chapter in education, the Roundtable and our constituents believe that arts education is among our strongest untapped resources to meeting this milestone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Each of the six core attributes starts with the arts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Research shows the impact of arts education on developing a broad range of in-demand skills that help students prepare not only for college, but career and civic life as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: As a theater educator, I saw firsthand as my students demonstrated their knowledge by writing and performing original musicals on topics like immigration, Rosa Parks, civil rights, as well as black inventors like Lonnie Johnson and more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Historically, these Regents exams have squeezed dance, music, theater, visual arts out of the school day in an attempt to teach to the test.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Moving away from these high-stakes testings towards alternative assessment measures is a positive shift that has immense potential to showcase student rigor, excellence, and creativity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Yet to realize this vision, we need more information and action from New York City public schools in four key areas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: First, we need clear guidance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: We need explicit clarity on how arts will be mapped within Portrait of a Graduate and how arts-based performance measures will count towards graduation requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Then we need more arts teachers and support for these teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Roughly one in five New York City public schools lack a certified arts teacher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: We must invest in the hiring of certified arts teachers to ensure that schools have the content knowledge on hand to support the delivery of arts integration and arts-based capstones projects.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Third, we need professional development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Arts teachers can't carry this load on their own.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: New York City Public Schools needs to invest in robust professional development so that educators can co-design these learning experiences and capstone experiences as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
