utterances.text: Last, we need strategic partnerships, leveraging DCLA, MoM, and New York City Public Schools, as well as our arts and cultural partners to support CTE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kimberly Olsen
utterances.text: Pathways.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank this panel for their testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm just kidding.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And again, as always, if I mispronounce your name, I apologize.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz calls Imanita Sanchez, Timothy Barba, Beth Fertig, E.T. Rodriguez, Kevin Benoit, and Iker Chiquitaco to testify.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls next panel including journalists and educators

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Imanita Sanchez, Timothy Barba, Beth Vertig, E.T.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Rodriguez,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Kevin Benoit or Benoit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'll tell you why I mispronounced it in a second.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Iker Chiquitaco.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I had a colleague whose last name was spelled the same way as Benoit.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: He didn't pronounce it as you pronounce it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I had a 50-50 shot.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Got it wrong.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You almost be friends.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You have like eight seats there and you're like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, please, Beth.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Beth Fertig, Executive Director of Press Pass NYC, says student journalism builds critical thinking, communication, and global citizenship. She asks for funding to train teachers through advisor fellowships so schools can build newsrooms.
chapters.title: Beth Fertig urges funding to train journalism teachers in public schools

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Hi.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: So thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: It's great to be here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: I'm Beth Ferdig, Executive Director of Press Pass NYC, which is part of the Youth Journalism Coalition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And before this job, I was a reporter for over 25 years at WNYC Public Radio, where I covered education and politics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: So I have been on the other side of this microphone a lot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And I want to tell you how much I love this organization and why it's relevant here, because Press Pass trains teachers and students to build school newsrooms in public schools across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: We've worked with more than 40 middle and high schools since launching five years ago, including Bronx River High School, Queens Tech, and a few of the other schools that are out there rallying with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And student journalism, as you've heard, is one of the most powerful and overlooked tools the city has for building the skills at Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Three pillars in particular, critical thinking, effective communicating, and being a global citizen, are constantly practiced in student newsrooms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: I've watched this happen at our partner schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: A Bronx student won a prestigious award for reporting on immigration enforcement in her neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: A student in East New York, Brooklyn, used real reporting to debunk a rumor about a school lockdown being caused by ICE.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: A student at a school in Queens told me interviewing people taught him the difference between writing news and opinion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And we are very grateful for the continued investment in student journalism, but we just want to plead for training the teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: That requires its own type of funding because you can't ask an English or social studies teacher to start a news team without sufficient training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Journalism is its own profession.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: The students need to learn the difference between news and opinion, ethics and understanding, how to talk to sources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And that's why a trained advisor to work with a student newsroom is so important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Our advisor fellowship gives teachers 30 hours of professional development, a mentor, and a stipend for free in their first year with two more years of support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: So this is how to build the infrastructure for student journalism by training teachers, and that's how to get what we want for all of our graduates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And we look forward to any collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: E.T. Rodriguez, journalist, professor, and Press Pass project manager, says his college students lack curiosity and public speaking skills. He says Regents are not necessary and calls for dedicated journalism teachers and a Bronx Journalism Hub.
chapters.title: E.T. Rodriguez says journalism should be in schools and teachers need training

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Hi, how are you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Hello, Council and Eric Dinowitz, who I know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: My name is E.T.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Rodriguez.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: I'm actually a professional journalist as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: I received a letter of recognition from Councilman Dinowitz when I resigned as editor-in-chief of the Rivadale Press.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: I'm also a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: project manager with Press Pass NYC, and I'm also a professor at Lehman College.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: So as a journalist, I lead my classes with a lot of news-based articles, and I tell my students to have a curiosity for the world around them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: My students are fresh out of high school, presumably with their Regents diploma, and an overwhelming amount of them do not have a curiosity for the environment around them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: They don't know what's going on in their own neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: They are cripplingly shy, suffering from public speaking skills, and they do not know how to put their thoughts on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: But as a workshop leader with Press Pass NYC, I have seen smart and articulate students, a lot like the ones that you've seen today, who are civically engaged young adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: And I know we celebrated $280,000 of investment in teaching.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: However, most of those schools, as Beth has said, don't have a dedicated journalism teacher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: And they have to pull from their faculty who are already busy and overwhelmed with teaching their classes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: So we, as she said, we offer three years of training and support for free to the teachers whose schools agree to give them the journalism class or club, which has enabled us to build back student press in more than 40 schools and counting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: You know, our program also, we're going to try to set up a Bronx Journalism Hub, which we're announcing in January, which I'm leading the project for, in a historically under-resourced neighborhood and in an area that's already being considered a media desert, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Bronx Times down to one full-time reporter, News Bronx 12 on a skeleton crew, and Norwood News just, you know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: And on this hiatus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: So, yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Yes, journalism in schools is important, but it's also important to train the teachers so that these students can be effective, civically engaged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Also, I dropped out of high school, didn't take my regents, failed my regents three times, went to school, got my bachelor's, got my master's.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Here I am today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - E.T. Rodriguez
utterances.text: Regents aren't necessary.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I also want to point out the Norwood News is in my district.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It was one of like two papers in my district, the other one being Viridale Press.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And yes, Norwood News shut down.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Very harmful to the community, for sure.

chapters.summary: Kevin Benoit, school program manager at Press Pass NYC, says journalism builds critical thinking, communication, and civic engagement. He has worked in schools across Brooklyn and Queens and says no one-size-fits-all approach will work without trained teachers and support.
chapters.title: Kevin Benoit says journalism teaches Portrait skills but needs administrative support

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I'm Kevin Benoit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: I am a Brooklyn resident, Brooklyn native.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: I am also the school program manager for Press Pass, so I'll definitely be doubling down what we've been saying here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Portrait of a Graduate sets out to support students so that they are critical thinkers, effective communicators, global citizens, and ready to learn, work, grow, create, and contribute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Student journalism checks all those boxes in real-time, hands-on ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: When a student reports a story, they investigate, verify facts, and weigh competing accounts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: That is critical thinking in action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: When they write, edit, and publish for their peers, they practice clear communication for a real audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: And when they're reporting, tackle civic questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Such as the student news team debunking rumors about immigration enforcement in their school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: or investigating practical impact of citywide phone bank, they act as engaged global citizens who are accountable for what they publish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: However, what I've witnessed in schools over the years is that student journalism requires support from local government and school administrators to thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: While media and technology involve, the fundamental principles of journalism remain constant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: It's important that we have programs that introduce students to meaningful journalism, teach fundamental principles, and provide a support system of trained teachers and administrators who are excited to build student newsroom.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Press Pass NYC does just that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: I've worked in schools in Canarsie, East Flatbush, Williamsburg, Bushwick, Jamaica, Queens, Crown Heights, etc., etc.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: What I will say is there is no one-size-fits-all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: And I think that is one of the things we heard today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: There's a lot that needs to be figured out and hopefully will be figured out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Hopefully the council continues to push back on some of the things you heard today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Journalism is one of the aspects that can help with portrait to graduate, but there is so much more that needs to be figured out.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks what role nonprofits can play in developing rigorous assessments. Beth Fertig says Press Pass trains teachers and follows up in schools. Kevin Benoit says schools need common standards so students across neighborhoods are judged on the same basis.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks panel how nonprofit partners can help develop assessments and rubrics

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I could tell you, this is, you know, when I became chair of the education committee, I said, like, I know we have to have a hearing on this issue because I kind of felt I knew where we would be, which is.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Not sure where, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So this is not the end of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Everyone here who's testified and beyond will be an integral part of, you know, making sure all the things we're asking for, whether it's the communication, whether it's the rigor, you know, whether the professional development, we're going to hold the DEWE accountable to make sure that's all there.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I do want to ask, though.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Supervising Superintendent Chang, I think, as well as the other superintendent who's here, spoke about partnerships with nonprofits and industry.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm wondering from your perspective, what obligation you feel or what role you play

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: you think you should or can have in developing the sort of assessments and rubrics that would demonstrate the level of rigor and engagement per the portrait of the graduate?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: You know, we're a service provider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: We train teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: We also have fellowships for students each semester.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: But in our work to train the teachers, we certainly follow through on what they're doing each semester.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: That's Kevin's whole job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: We hired him just now.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just today?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And you already put him up on the panel?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: I'd say a month ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: But he'd been working with us already for a few years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And now his full-time job is being that person who checks out whether our– we have journalism educators who train the teachers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Kevin's job is going to the schools to make sure that–

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: They're not hitting too many roadblocks because they need a lot of support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: And that's why our fellowship gives them two more years beyond that, because it's really hard to learn a whole profession, journalism, and then teach a bunch of kids how to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: So when you're asking really about...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Rubrics or what I'm asking is that is we're talking about portfolios we talk about some sort of assessment you've heard it mentioned throughout the day some sort of assessment and some sort of assurances that you know a kid from Canarsie

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: is doing the same type of work and it's held to the same standard as a kid

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: From Bedford Park.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Now I get what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: So, all right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Beth Fertig
utterances.text: Kevin, Kevin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: So outside of Press Pass, I've also worked in education for 20 years from Harlem Children's Zone to you name it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: I worked in high school for five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: I was a career and all that to say what I've seen this summer alone, I have 50 interns, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Coming from city schools all over the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: The biggest issue is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: While they can all come up and say how great their school is, oftentimes they don't even know what's happening at the school up the block or in the same building.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: So unless we can figure out a way to get all the schools on the same page, you know, we're all going to do journalism.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: We're all going, and it doesn't have to be journalism, but we're all going to do the same things so that we're all judged on the same basis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Because even with regents, right, and again, I worked at a high school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: We knew if we had students with IEPs, all we had to do was get them to take the test three times, even if they failed at all three.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: As long as you took it three times, we can ask the city to just waive it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: And this was happening with most of the black and brown students that I worked with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: But then I go to a Bronx Science or a Brooklyn Tech, and they look at the regents like, this is just one of the things we have to do today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: And they're going to do 15 other things, and they're going to be successful at all 15, but then you have the same...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: Students who live on the same block with them go to the same corner store, and they're not getting the same services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: So unless we can figure out how we can get everyone on that same page, and I think it starts at some of our local schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: It starts with some of our smaller districts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kevin Benoit
utterances.text: But overall, there's no reason a student in Canarsie isn't getting the same education as someone in Park Slope.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah, agreed.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I would hope and think that if, you know, the DOE shouldn't be creating their whatever assessments, whatever portfolio they're asking the kids to do, they shouldn't be doing that in silos, that you have expertise in journalism,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: that you can and should be partners with the DOE in that work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You know best what good journalism looks like.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I would just hope and think the DOE would lean on you for that and that you it seems like you are willing and able partners in that work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz calls Edgar Rodriguez, AJ Rothman Noonan, Lara Evangelista, David Adams, and Aurora Kushner to testify.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls next panel of affinity network leaders

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank this panel and call up the next panel.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Edgar Rodriguez, AJ Rothman Noonan, Lara Evangelista, David Adams, and Aurora Kushner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I don't have mine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: I'm going to submit it online.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin when ready.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Edgar Rodriguez, VP at New Visions for Public Schools, says schools must reorganize teaching and assessment but teachers lack training. He says affinity organizations serve a third of high schools and have field-tested project-based curriculum ready to support the transition.
chapters.title: Edgar Rodriguez says New Visions curriculum and affinity partners are ready to support Portrait

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, the Novets and panel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: My name is Edgar Rodriguez, and before this role, I served for over 20 years as a teacher, assistant principal, and principal of our schools in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: I come here today as vice president of school support and innovations for public schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Which has partnered with the city for over 37 years to drive system-level change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: As an affinity partner, we're the lead partner for 71 public high schools and provide services for schools across the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: The shift associated with Portrait of a Graduate asks schools to reorganize and educators to teach and assess students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: In ways that they've never been trained to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: As educators who are concerned that so many questions remain unanswered, even as these changes are being implemented as we speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Students whose diplomas will be granted under the new requirements are already in our buildings, taught by teachers who have received

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: little relevant professional learning in this matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Generative AI brings opportunities and at the same time lots of challenges and questions about the validity of any assessment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: This work has to move quickly and it has to draw on the capacity that already exists in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Affinity organizations represented in this panel

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: collectively serve a third of the high schools in the city and represent a significant piece of that capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: We have spent decades doing this work with our schools, and the system should treat us as critical resource in this transition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: New Visions Affinity Network and our work with schools

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: has derived three key things that we believe are of value to this transition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Curriculum, we have produced curriculum in science and social studies that is used by the majority of high schools across the city, and it's based on real-world investigations and phenomena,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: and it's a type of project-based learning that the Portuguese graduate calls for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: It's already written, goes through continuous revisions, and it's already field tested.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: The rest is in my...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: Didn't make the two minutes, but I'll do better next time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I also want to appreciate New Visions.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I taught at a New Vision school, so double thank you.

chapters.summary: David Adams, CEO of Urban Assembly, says Portrait aligns with Urban Assembly's work in social-emotional learning and post-secondary readiness. His network's class of 2024 had a 90.3% graduation rate, and he offers to test, codify, and scale practices.
chapters.title: David Adams offers Urban Assembly as innovation and scaling partner

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Good afternoon, evening, Chair Denowitz.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: I want to, first of all, thank you for all your support for the Finney Network and Urban Assembly, as well as being a champion for social emotional development of our young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: I am David Adams, Chief Executive Officer at the Urban Assembly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: For 30 years, the Urban Assembly has partnered with New York City Public Schools to design, test, and scale solutions for students historically underserved by our education system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Today, our network includes 23 unscreened career-connected middle and high schools, and we support the approach of the graduate because it recognizes that readiness requires more than just credits and exams, that students must learn to think critically, communicate effectively, build relationships,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: navigate decisions, and apply their real-world learning to real-world challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: This vision closely reflects Urban Assembly's work in social and emotional learning, post-secondary readiness, and instructional quality, and our students demonstrate what is possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Our class of 24 achieved a 90.3% graduation rate, seven points above the city rate, and particularly strong outcomes from black and Latin students, multilingual learners, and students with disabilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: The Urban Assembly has demonstrated a strong record of helping New York City public schools moving promising ideas to scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Through Strong Resilient NYC, we helped make social and emotional learning support available across 1,600 schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: We trained more than 50,000 educators and supported assessment for more than 720,000 students.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: We helped develop post-secondary bridge model that ultimately expanded citywide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: And we now support Future Ready NYC in connecting academic learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: to college and career pathways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: These experiences have taught us that a strong vision is only the beginning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Schools need practical tools, professional learning, implementation support, meaningful measures of student growth, and systems for learning what works.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Urban Assembly is ready to bring that experience to the portrait of a graduate as an innovation and scaling partner

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: that can test approaches in real schools, examine the evidence, codify effective practices, and help New York City public schools bring them to students across the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: I was watching that the other day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Across the country, wow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: You have big goals.

chapters.summary: AJ Rathmann-Noonan, Executive Director of the NY Performance Standards Consortium, says changing assessment requires reorienting school culture, top-down support for bottom-up reform, and lateral accountability. She invites the Council to moderation studies and intervisitation days.
chapters.title: AJ Rathmann-Noonan shares consortium lessons for scaling performance assessment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Hi, Chair Dinnowitz, and thank you for the support you've shown us already today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: My name is AJ Rathbuninen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: I'm Executive Director of the New York Performance Standards Consortium.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: As you've heard, we're a homegrown model built by NYC educators for NYC students, a performance assessment that holds students to high standards.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: My written testimony also includes information about our assessment system and its alignment to the New York State portrait.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: The consortium began almost 30 years ago when New York City Superintendent Steve Phillips and Deborah Meyer sought state approval for a group of schools to use performance assessment instead of regents exams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: It was a founder and the DOE has effectively supported the consortium ever since.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: As the rest of the system continued to use Regents exams, first through the alternative high school district, then the CFN structure, and now the affinity schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: report without which we couldn't have built and sustained this system or welcome 10 new schools in 2013.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: We've learned many lessons.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: I'll share three today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: First, changing assessment is just the start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: It requires reorienting school culture towards inquiry, all of which takes extensive professional development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: and collaboration led by teachers, not outside vendors and consultants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: So the system is truly owned by the educators.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Second, this work cannot be dictated from the top.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: The school system must instead provide what Commissioner Tom Sobel called top-down support for bottom-up school reform, like funding and structures that provide for collaboration, exactly what Affinity's partnership model enables, and school-based decision-making through programs like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: PROS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Third, high standards require accountability, but not the top-down test-based accountability we've relied on for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: It requires lateral accountability within and across schools and to the communities that schools serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: The DOE can help by building more networks like Affinity and aligning incentives, including city dashboards, away from test scores and towards more robust measures of school quality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Finally, I invite you and the council staff to see our work firsthand.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: In October, our teachers hold half-day moderation studies to calibrate scoring of student work, the heart of our PD.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: And in November and December, our network hosts intervisitation days.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Dates and RSVP information are at the bottom of my written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Wow, that's a very, very fast last sentence.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I love it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Now, my favorite thing you said was that we have the expertise here in our city, that we don't need to hire outside vendors to do this work at great cost and probably lesser quality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Can I ask you this other letter?

chapters.summary: Aurora Kushner, VP at NYC Outward Bound Schools, says moving away from Regents does not dilute rigor. Outward Bound's project-based units, advisory structure, and presentations of learning produce strong graduation, enrollment, and climate outcomes.
chapters.title: Aurora Kushner says Outward Bound schools show rigor through performance assessment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Aurora Kushner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: I'm the Vice President of Programs at New York City Outward Bound Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Chair Danowitz, thank you for this hearing and thank you for all the support for Outward Bound that you've given us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: For over 30 years, we have partnered with New York City Public Schools to pioneer the exact kind of powerful learning defined by New York State Inspires as we transition towards the portrait of a graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: As New York moves from single-day, high-stakes regents exams towards performance-based assessments and broader measures of student learning, some worry that academic rigor will be diluted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Our research-based approach shows that this is a false choice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Through our affinity network, our schools, all of our schools, are living laboratories for this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: We coach educators to design rigorous, standards-aligned, project-based units grounded in real-world problem-solving where students analyze, synthesize, and apply complex concepts rather than simply memorize information.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: We also build student agency and belonging through our signature advisory structure, CRU, where every student is known, valued, mentored, and held accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Students track their own progress, identify learning targets, and publicly demonstrate their growth through presentations of learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: and performance-based assessments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: When you intentionally pair meaningful challenge and real-world engagement with genuine belonging, students thrive and the results are measurable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: We see that in our graduation rates, we see that in our post-secondary enrollment and our persistence data.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Far surpassing city averages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: Our DOE climate surveys consistently outperform the city in academic rigor and trust.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: This transition is not about lowering expectations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: It's about expanding what rigor means and giving students more ways to demonstrate what they know and what they can do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: We don't need to start from scratch.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: The teacher coaching practices, school models, and student outcome data are already here in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: We invite you to come visit our partner schools, see crew.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I can finish sentence for you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Again, because I have already had the great pleasure of visiting your schools, and I will surely be happy to do even more visits.

chapters.summary: Laura Evangelista, Executive Director of Internationals Network and former principal of Flushing International, describes shifting to performance-based assessments requiring six defended tasks. She says this deepened rigor and used affinity district structures for professional learning.
chapters.title: Laura Evangelista says Internationals Network transformed graduation to performance-based system

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Dinowitz and members of the Education Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: My name is Laura Evangelista.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of Internationals Network for Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: For over 20 years, we've partnered with New York City Public Schools to design and support schools for newly arrived immigrant students through a practitioner-developed and research-based approach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: I'm also a New York City retired educator and the former principal of Flushing International High School, where in 2013, I led the transition from a regents-based

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: graduation requirement to a fully performance-based assessment system requiring students to complete and publicly defend six rigorous tasks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: What I learned is that this shift is not simply about replacing exams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: It's about transforming instruction and students'everyday experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: Preparing students for graduation defenses begins in the ninth grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: I had to have teachers collaborating across subjects and grade levels to develop students'abilities to research, investigate questions, revise their work, and defend their thinking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: We didn't abandon any academic rigor or content when we did this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: We deepened it while developing the competencies that now the New York State Portrait of a Graduate holds.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: And we extended that learning beyond the classroom through work-based learning, dual enrollment, giving students to...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: opportunity to apply their knowledge, explore careers and those skills in the world and college level work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: And we could not have done this work alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: International's network worked alongside our schools to strengthen instruction, develop common rubrics, and build accountability across the network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: The creation of the Affinity District in 2015

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: deepen that work by aligning district resources and accountability with our practitioner expertise and sustain professional learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: The affinity structure has made ambitious reforms possible in everyday classrooms and sustains them over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: Today, 17 international schools demonstrate what's possible when schools have the expertise, support, and accountability to sustain the work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: As we implement the New York Portrait of a Graduate, we stand ready to work with NYCPS and invite you to our schools.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz asks if DOE has leaned on affinity partners enough. David Adams says superintendent accountability is not organized around scaling or innovation. Edgar Rodriguez says work with the Office of Pathways on metrics is flourishing but not explicitly tied to Portrait.
chapters.title: Dinowitz asks affinity leaders if DOE leverages their expertise enough

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I don't want to thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I mean, I think all of you in your different ways have supported the work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I've done the work of this council, whether it's panels with your students, particularly the international schools, I think have done a lot for obviously our immigrant students.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But all of you in various ways have supported the students and this council and our work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You were mentioned in the DOE's testimony, the work the DOE does with you, getting an understanding, getting expertise on what the portrait could be.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: In your opinion, has the DOE leaned on you hard enough for that support?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Have they utilized the skill set that you bring to the table enough?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: I think there's a lot more work to be done in terms of coordination with the DEA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: Each of our schools has a superintendent that works with our schools directly, but that superintendent accountability is not organized around scaling or innovation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: It's organized around the same kind of accountability structures that other superintendents are organized around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: For us to be able to take the practices that we have developed and ensure that all students have access to them,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - David Adams
utterances.text: the superintendent structure that goes up to the DEWE needs to see themselves as innovators and problem solvers to the questions of things like Portrait of the Graduate rather than just operational executors around what the DEWE's objective is.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I think sort of related to what AJ says, and kind of what I talk about all the time, it's like, what are you measuring?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: If you're measuring those region scores, credit accrual, and attendance, that's how you're going to measure success.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But if you have a measure of success for innovation, then I think we would probably start seeing a lot more of that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Do you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Aurora Kushner
utterances.text: I was going to add that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: There is, I mean, this is very complex.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: All afternoon we've been talking about, like, all the layers, these touches, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: And so there's a piece around, you know, assessment, away with the regions, performance-based assessments as one piece.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: There's another piece around work-based learning, work-based readiness, and we're doing a lot of collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: With the Office of Pathways around Future Ready and how the portal can assist monitoring the progress with all those metrics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: I think that work has been flourishing, not explicitly in the context of portrait, but I think it can inform it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: And it's one area in which we're collaborating in terms of like our work innovations and how the portal has served as a place for schools, districts, and the central office to kind of take a look at where the schools stand, where the individual students stand,

chapters.summary: Dinowitz concludes the panel is ready to work but DOE is not leveraging their skills enough. AJ Rathmann-Noonan says educators are willing to share and points to DOE staff connected to consortium schools. Laura Evangelista says schools hosted visitations before and will again.
chapters.title: Dinowitz says affinity partners are ready but need DOE structure and investment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edgar Rodriguez
utterances.text: and the plans that have to happen to respond to those patterns.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So I'm seeing a panel of people who stand ready to work.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: With the DOE, who are not being, whose skills and experience are not being leveraged enough,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: and who also, in order to support that, need the DOE to recognize some of the kind of special work that the Affinity Network does, and I guess rate the schools,

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: on that or value that sort of work as part of their quality review, let's say.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: I mean, I think the other important thing to say is that the educators in our schools are really

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: passionate about the work that they do and really willing to share.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: And I think as we wait for New York City public schools to figure out what the build out of the transition is going to look like and how they're going to think about how classroom instruction will change and sort of how high school look different, there are people who are ready to be tapped.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: There were multiple people on this panel from New York City Public Schools today that are connected to our schools, right, including Alan Chang, including Delia Bebe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: Like, these are people that know our work, and they know we're ready to help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alexandra (AJ) Rathmann-Noonan
utterances.text: And so I think it'll come eventually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: And I think historically, when there have been, like you alluded to, the programs in the past about the visitations, inter-visitations, when we look at all the previous structures, Showcase, Learning Partners,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Laura Evangelista
utterances.text: Lighthouse, I mean, overwhelmingly, our schools were willing to host folks during those and again are willing to do it again.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But as I kind of mentioned towards the end, it takes the structure from the DOE and it takes investment and money, right?

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Like the support investment, the money investment, it takes all that.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: But it's good to know that we have a whole network of partners.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And we're going to keep making sure the DOE knows it and acts on it.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'd like to thank this panel for their testimony today.

utterances.text: Well, I'll get it right the third time.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I promise.

utterances.text: Edward Gordon, Nadav Zimer, and Kamala Carmen.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: I'm going to mix things up, you know, go a little crazy.

utterances.text: We'll start on the right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen

chapters.summary: Kamala Carmen, parent of two consortium graduates, says her children attained Portrait attributes through inquiry-based, performance-assessed schooling. She opted them out of state tests and criticizes NYC Reads and Solves as corporate curriculum.
chapters.title: Parent Kamala Carmen says consortium model already achieves Portrait outcomes

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Sure is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: My name is Kamala Carmen, and I'm the parent of two children, both now in their early 20s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: I believe that my children graduated from their New York City public 6 through 12 school, having fully attained the attributes distributed around the portrait of a graduate wheel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: That they did so is arguably a foregone conclusion since they attended a consortium school, and the practices and approaches of the consortium model, as you heard today, very intentionally aim for the outcomes called for by Portrait of a Graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: Moreover, even their prior schooling was pointing my kids in this direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: Brooklyn New School, their progressive public elementary school, in many ways resembled what a consortium school for younger children might look like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: It, too, used an inquiry approach to nurture students'curiosity, encourage collaboration with peers, and foster independent critical thinking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: It, too, lived by the maxim, more teaching and learning, less testing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: I'm thrilled that at long last, New York State has moved to decouple the Regents exams from graduation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: I know that this change raises alarms for some parents and pundits who worry that this means that standards will be lowered or feel panic about what will replace the Regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: I'm here to tell you that I opted my children out of nearly every state test in elementary and middle school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: It would have been all, but the opt-out movement wasn't really a thing until my older child was in sixth grade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: Because of the consortium's waiver, my older child took only the ELA Regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: My younger child didn't even take that due to COVID cancellation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: Far from lowered standards, what I saw at both my children's school were environments that helped them prepare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: work that was far more challenging and detailed and meaningful than what the state tests or the regents would have asked of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: They didn't need any external replacement assessments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: They just needed schools where teachers were honored as professionals with plenty of opportunities to advance their own learning and practice, and students were not seen merely as data points with no agency in shaping their learning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: The actual threat to high standards is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: Hello?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: The actual threat to high standards is not the diminution of the regents'exams, but the imposition on schools of the bland corporate curriculum products of New York City Reads and Solves and the incessant and invasive screeners students today are surveilled with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: I am relieved my kids graduated before that sad state of affairs came to pass.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: And that's, again, the outside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kamala Carmen
utterances.text: We don't need outside curriculum for millions of dollars.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Testing, testing.

chapters.summary: Edward Gordon, president of Nubian Conservatory of Music and a former NYC teacher, argues rap has few redeeming qualities and should not be brought into schools. He calls for orchestras, choruses, bands, and repair of a school organ.
chapters.title: Edward Gordon criticizes rap in schools and calls for music programs

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: It's on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Chairman of the committee, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: My name is Edward Gordon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: I'm the president of the Nubian Conservatory of Music.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: It is a small private music school in Brooklyn, New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: I come to you as an educator of over 50 years experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: And 31 of those years were spent in the classrooms of the New York City public school system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: I am a former parent of the New York school system and now a grandparent of the New York school system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Mayor Mumdani wants to bring rap poetry into the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: I have expressed in writing why I do not think that that is a good idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: If we are speaking honestly about rap, it has very few redeeming qualities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: No one is learning how to sing properly, how to play an instrument.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Many of the people that it glorifies are either ex-drug dealers or ex-convicts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Please don't get me wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: I am all for giving people a second chance, but I was taught that role models have to be held to a higher standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: And we have wonderful role models out there, such as Mariah Carey or Lawrence Brownlee, the African-American metropolitan opportunist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: We see young men holding their groins for periods of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: And there is the filthy language which often degrades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: It's black people and especially black women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: The bottom line is that a 10-year-old black boy was trampled to death at a so-called rap concert.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: I want something better for my granddaughter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Our children need orchestras, choruses, and bands.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Erasmus Hall High School has an electronic organ sitting there collecting dust, but it needs about $2,000 worth of work to make it fully functional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: That figure is probably higher by now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Sorry, my sinuses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: Oh, as I got that estimate a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: No one wants to help me raise money.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Just finish up your last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Edward Gordon
utterances.text: No one wants to help me raise money to repair that instrument.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And, you know, we heard, I think, one other person talk about the arts, and I think the arts...

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Can and should be integrated into the portrait of a graduate as well.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: For me, at least, my own personal experience, someone who, you know, theater and music was integral to my middle and high school experience and someone who then as a teacher saw theater and music as something that was transformative for my students.

chapters.summary: Alisa Uchaikina, a senior at Kingsborough Early College, says her school lacks a journalism club but a fellowship let her write about topics she cares about and find her voice. She asks DOE to support journalism education in all schools.
chapters.title: Alisa Uchaikina says journalism fellowship gave her voice and asks for expansion

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: This can and should be part of the portrait of the graduate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: Hello, my name is Alisa Ochaikina.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: I'm a senior at Kingsborough Early College Secondary School, and I'm a student from Brooklyn, New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: My school doesn't have a dedicated journalist club, but one of the opportunities my school gave me was the Fellowship for the Future of Journalists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: I first applied to the program during my sophomore year, and this is actually one of the reasons I'm here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: The program gave me the opportunity to explore journalism from different angles and perspectives, as well as to meet a lot of amazing journalists and learn from their experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: Our mentors don't teach us how to follow templates or put strong limitations on our creativity and our words, which what school usually does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: Instead, we have the freedom to write about things that generally interest us and find our own voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: One of the articles I wrote this year is called How the Morning Shapes the Mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: In this article, I talk about the importance of reducing our use of phones, especially during the first 30 minutes after waking up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: It can give your brain a calmer start to the day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: That way you can feel more present, which is important for students while taking regents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: And if it wasn't for journalists, I might have never thought about something like this or decided to experiment with it in my own life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: Journalists help me notice things I might normally overlook and sell interesting stories about things that I can seem ordinary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: It gives me freedom to explore what I genuinely care about, find people who share those interests, and develop my own voice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for everything this program has given me, which is why it's very sad to know that so many students don't have the same opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: I believe every student

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: should have the chance to write, learn from professionals, and have their voice heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: Journalism teaches us critical thinking by asking questions and looking at different perspectives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: And it teaches effective communications by turning our ideas into stories that others can understand and connect with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: I'm just asking to make sure that DOE supports journalism education and opportunities like Fellowship for the Future of Journalism in all NYC public schools, or at least most of them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: So every student has the chance to develop their voice, learn from professionals, and have their stories heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alisa Uchaikina
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Nadav Zeimer, a former physics teacher and principal, argues Regents create perverse incentives and AI makes take-home essays unreliable. He calls for validated video portfolios and expanding journalism so students have authentic audiences and become creators, not scrollers.
chapters.title: Nadav Zeimer calls for validated video portfolios and real audiences for students

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: You may begin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Chair Dynowitz, thank you for, and committee, thank you for this opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: I taught physics and led Harlem Renaissance Transfer High School through a period of turnaround.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: The difference in our system was never talent and opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: It's always been audience, and audience has always been rationed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: You saw, you have said yourself that the Regents create perverse incentives, and audience is what replaces them, is what I'm arguing here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Assign an essay that only one teacher will read and the student lets AI write it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Put her on stage defending her own work and no one can stand in for her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Would you let your own children be assessed by an auditorium full of chatbots?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: All students deserve an authentic audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Anything less and AI will lure them into offloading their learning and our public schools will crumble as a result.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: The answer to AI is not more ed tech.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: It's an expert human audience for every student.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Video is the new number two pencil.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Learning happens off screen and in the real world, and the camera comes out to capture their off screen learning for assessment purposes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: In video format, student work can be reproduced and distributed across space and time at zero cost, allowing an expert reviewer or college admissions officer to pull up a chair to each student's proudest moments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: I support the moratorium as a tourniquet, not a solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Portfolios for all is the solution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: It's the only solution since everything is downstream of assessment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: And the only way to offer an expert audience to all students is validated video portfolios.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Real work validated by experts at scale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: The first step is journalism, which gives students an audience, a deadline, and a reason to check facts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Let's expand J4A and let student creators know that we support them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: For example, we can give student journalists a press pass within school that allows them to use electronic devices to create content, not consume it as journalists.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Let's ensure New York City students learn to be creators, not scrollers, drivers of AI, not dependents on it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Give every student a real audience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: The research is in my written testimony with more detail, and you can find more at academiccapital.org.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Nadav Zeimer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: And I'm sure you tuned into our hearing last week and the one in June where we discussed extensively screen time and AI.

chapters.summary: Dinowitz calls Dominique Jones, Joni Rivera, Ellen McHugh, and Teresa Rainian to testify.
chapters.title: Dinowitz calls final in-person panel

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: So thank you for this panel's testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eric Dinowitz
utterances.text: Our final in-person panel, Dominique Jones, Joni Rivera, Ellen McHugh, Teresa Rainian.
